templates.title: Meeting join failures: first tries that failed, with quick retries collapsed
templates.subtopic: gaps and islands with LAG and a running SUM, first-row attributes, conditional aggregation

sections.scenario: A meetings product logs every attempt a person makes to join a meeting, from desktop apps, the web and phones. The reliability team wants one number per customer organisation (tenant) and client platform: of the people who tried to join, how many could not get in on their first try? A failure followed straight away by a successful retry is a blip, not a failed join, so retries within two minutes of the previous attempt are collapsed into one try. The sample has {{attempts}} attempts in one table.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns tenant_id, client_platform, participants, failed_first_try, recovered_later, failed_share, one row per tenant and platform, ordered by tenant_id, client_platform. A participant is one (meeting_id, user_id). Order a participant's attempts by attempt_ts, then attempt_id. A try starts at the first attempt and at every attempt more than 120 seconds after the participant's previous attempt; an attempt at most 120 seconds after the previous one belongs to the same try, so a chain of quick retries stays one try. The first try failed if none of its attempts has outcome = 'succeeded'. recovered_later counts participants whose first try failed and a later try succeeded. failed_share is failed_first_try / participants, rounded to 4 decimal places. A participant is counted once, on the client_platform of their first attempt. {{platform_rule}} {{cancel_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). tenant_id is the meeting's tenant and is the same on every attempt of a meeting. The 120 seconds are exact, measured between attempt_ts values.
sections.assumptions: Tenants are fictional sample organisations; meetings, users, timings and outcomes are hypothetical. Real clients report richer error codes; the two outcomes and the two-minute rule are this exercise's definitions.
sections.criteria: Participant grain is (meeting_id, user_id); tries split on a gap of more than 120 seconds from the previous attempt (chained, inclusive at 120); a first try fails only if none of its attempts succeeded; recovered_later only from later tries; the platform of the first attempt with the attempt_id tie-break (Hard+); cancelled attempts removed before tries are built and the floor applied (Very Hard); correct rounding and order; can discuss clock skew, late data and incremental sessionisation.

clarifications.q: Is the two-minute window measured from the first attempt of the try or from the previous attempt?
clarifications.a: From the previous attempt. Three attempts 100 seconds apart are one try, although the last is 200 seconds after the first.

clarifications.q: An attempt exactly 120 seconds after the previous one?
clarifications.a: Same try. Only a gap of more than 120 seconds starts a new try.

clarifications.q: The same person joins two meetings in one afternoon.
clarifications.a: Two participants, each with their own first try.

clarifications.q: The first attempt failed and a retry 30 seconds later succeeded.
clarifications.a: The first try succeeded; this participant is not in failed_first_try.

clarifications.q: The first try failed and the person never got in.
clarifications.a: Counted in failed_first_try, not in recovered_later.

hints: LAG(attempt_ts) per (meeting_id, user_id) flags the attempts that start a new try; a running SUM of that flag numbers the tries (gaps and islands).
Reduce to one row per participant: the platform of row number 1, whether try 1 had a success, whether any later try had one. Then aggregate per tenant and platform.
BOOL_OR(…) FILTER (WHERE …) is NULL when the filter matches no row; wrap it in COALESCE.
followups: The team also wants the median time from the first attempt to getting in, for participants whose first try failed. What would you add?
Client clocks can be minutes off and some attempts arrive a day late. How do try boundaries and the daily report change?
A tenant reports that their failure share doubled after a client update, but they had 12 participants. How would you show uncertainty, and when would you hold a group back?
At billions of attempts a day, how would you build tries incrementally when a try can straddle the boundary between two processing batches?

rules.ask: Your LAG compares each attempt with the previous one. What is in its ORDER BY, and what happens when two attempts share a timestamp?
Someone fails on the web and gets in from the desktop app 20 seconds later. Which platform are they counted on, and which row does your query take it from?
Fixed two-minute buckets put attempts at 10:01:59 and 10:02:01 into different tries. How does your rule avoid that?
The same person joins two meetings. Are they one participant or two, and what does your GROUP BY say?
A cancelled attempt sits between a failure and a success 200 seconds apart. Does it link them into one try in your query?

templates.title: Update ring compliance: installs within N days of the first offer
templates.subtopic: per-entity windows, EXISTS with inclusive bounds, point-in-time lookup, NULL-safe ratios

sections.scenario: An organisation's IT team rolls operating-system quality updates out in rings: a small preview or pilot group first, the broad population last. For each ring and OS build they track how many offered devices installed the update within a set number of days. A laptop that sat switched off in a drawer for the whole period says nothing about the rollout, so devices that were never online in the period are excluded from the rate rather than counted as failures. You have devices, their build history, offers, installs and check-ins for {{devices}} devices, and the report is for update {{update_id}} within {{days}} days.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns ring, os_build, offered_devices, online_devices, compliant_devices, compliance_rate, one row per (ring, os_build) with at least one device offered {{update_id}}, ordered by ring, os_build. Each offered device has a window from its first offer of {{update_id}} to exactly {{days}} days later, both ends inclusive. The device is compliant if it has an install of {{update_id}} in the window, and online if it has a check-in in the window or is compliant (an install proves it was online). offered_devices counts every offered device; online_devices and compliant_devices count those that were online and compliant. os_build is the device's build at its first offer: the device_builds row with the latest effective_at at or before that offer. compliance_rate is compliant_devices / online_devices, rounded to 4 decimal places, and NULL when no device in the group was online. {{offer_rule}} {{build_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). The tables also hold offers and installs of other updates, and devices that were never offered this one. A check-in before the first offer or after the window does not make a device online.
sections.assumptions: Ring names, update ids, build numbers, dates and the compliance rule are hypothetical. Real update management adds deferrals, deadlines, pauses and restarts; they are out of scope here.
sections.criteria: Window from the first offer of this update, inclusive at both ends; installs of this update only; online means a check-in in the window or an install in the window; never-online devices kept in offered_devices but out of the denominator; NULL rate for an all-offline group (Hard+); the build in effect at the first offer from the history (Very Hard); deterministic order; can discuss compliance curves, lost check-ins, pauses and scale.

clarifications.q: A device was offered the update twice. Which offer starts the window?
clarifications.a: The first. A re-offer does not restart the clock.

clarifications.q: An install exactly N days after the first offer, to the second?
clarifications.a: Compliant. Both ends of the window are inclusive.

clarifications.q: A device installed in the window but has no check-in rows at all.
clarifications.a: It was online: installing proves it.

clarifications.q: A device checked in only before it was offered the update.
clarifications.a: It counts in offered_devices but was not online in the window, so it is not in the rate's denominator.

clarifications.q: Every device in a group was offline.
clarifications.a: Report the row anyway, with compliance_rate NULL.

hints: Build one row per offered device first: MIN(offered_at) as the start and the start plus INTERVAL '{{days}} days' as the end.
EXISTS subqueries with BETWEEN decide "installed this update in the window" and "checked in in the window" without multiplying rows.
The build at the offer is a "latest row at or before" lookup: a correlated subquery with ORDER BY effective_at DESC LIMIT 1, a LATERAL join, or DISTINCT ON.
NULLIF(online, 0) keeps an all-offline group from dividing by zero.
followups: The team wants a compliance curve: the cumulative share installed on day 0, 1, …, N after the offer, per ring. What changes?
Devices check in every few hours and some check-ins are lost. How would you estimate how many "never online" devices were in fact online?
A ring is paused for a week after a problem is found. Should paused days count against the N-day window, and how would you model the pause?
With tens of millions of devices and a check-in every few hours, which table dominates the cost, and what would you precompute so the report does not scan it each time?

rules.ask: A device was offered the update on Monday and again on Thursday. Which day starts its window in your query, and what does the rule say?
The device moved to a newer build after the offer. Which build does your report use, and why would the rollout team care?
Joining check-ins and installs onto devices multiplies rows. How do you make sure each device is counted once per group?
Is an install at exactly the end of the window inside it in your query? Show the comparison you used.
In a group where every device was offline, what does your rate show, and is 0 the honest answer?

templates.title: Copilot suggestions kept: accepted and not undone within five minutes
templates.subtopic: event matching inside a time window, per-entity deduplication, LEFT JOIN denominators, HAVING floors

sections.scenario: An AI assistant inside office apps offers inline suggestions: a rewritten sentence, a formula, a reply draft. Acceptance alone overstates how useful they are, because people accept a suggestion and press undo seconds later. The product team therefore tracks suggestions kept: accepted and not undone within five minutes. The report is per app and language, and small groups are noisy, so a group with fewer than {{min_shown}} suggestions shown is left out. The tables hold only event metadata: no prompt, suggestion or document text exists in them. The sample has {{suggestions}} suggestions.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns app, language, shown, accepted, kept, accept_rate, keep_rate, one row per (app, language) with at least {{min_shown}} suggestions shown, ordered by app, language. shown counts suggestions; accepted counts suggestions with at least one accepted event. A suggestion is kept if it was accepted and has no undone event after its last acceptance and at most 300 seconds after it (an undo exactly 300 seconds later is within five minutes). accept_rate is accepted / shown and keep_rate is kept / accepted (NULL when nothing was accepted), both rounded to 4 decimal places. dismissed events are not acceptances. {{accept_rule}} {{lang_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). Within one suggestion no two events share a timestamp. A suggestion with no events at all was shown and ignored.
sections.assumptions: Apps, languages, users, counts and timings are hypothetical, and the five-minute "kept" rule is this exercise's definition, not a published product metric. Events are client logs with one row per user action.
sections.criteria: One row per suggestion before aggregating; the clock runs from the last acceptance; the undo window is after the acceptance and inclusive at 300 seconds; a LEFT JOIN keeps unaccepted suggestions in shown; the floor on shown; NULL keep_rate when nothing was accepted; duplicate acceptances counted once (Hard+); re-acceptance after an undo and 'und' for a missing language (Very Hard); can discuss several windows at once, uneven client logging, small-group privacy and streaming corrections.

clarifications.q: An undo exactly 300 seconds after the acceptance?
clarifications.a: Within five minutes, so the suggestion is not kept.

clarifications.q: An undo 20 minutes later?
clarifications.a: Still kept. Only an undo within five minutes counts against it.

clarifications.q: Is the floor on suggestions shown or on suggestions accepted?
clarifications.a: Shown.

clarifications.q: Is keep_rate over shown or over accepted?
clarifications.a: Over accepted.

clarifications.q: Does a dismissed suggestion count in shown?
clarifications.a: Yes. Every row of suggestions was shown.

hints: Reduce the acceptance events to one row per suggestion first: its last acceptance time.
Start from suggestions with a LEFT JOIN, so suggestions with no events still count as shown, and test for an undo in (accepted_at, accepted_at + 5 minutes] with NOT EXISTS.
Apply the floor with HAVING COUNT(*) >= … on the per-suggestion rows, after grouping.
followups: The team wants "kept" at 1, 5 and 30 minutes side by side. How would you compute all three in one pass?
Only some clients log undo events. How would that bias keep_rate between apps, and how would you report it?
Tenant admins see this report for their own organisation. Which groups could reveal one person's behaviour, and what would you add beyond a floor on shown?
Events arrive as a stream, and a suggestion's outcome is final only five minutes after its last acceptance. How would you publish a daily number on time and correct it later?

rules.ask: Joining events to suggestions gives one row per event. A suggestion with two accepted events: how many times is it counted as accepted?
Accepted, accepted again 3 seconds later, then undone 299 seconds after the second. Which acceptance does your clock start from, and is the suggestion kept?
BETWEEN includes both ends. Which end of the undo window must be inclusive here, and does the other end matter?
What happens to suggestions with no detected language in your query?
Your floor is in HAVING. Is it counting suggestions shown, or rows produced by a join to events?

templates.title: Lobby matchmaking: the most 1v1 pairs within a skill gap
templates.subtopic: matching on a line, sliding-window maximum with a deque, lexicographic tie-breaks

sections.scenario: An online game's 1v1 mode keeps players in a lobby until it can pair them with an opponent of similar skill. Every few seconds the matchmaker takes a snapshot of the lobby and pairs as many players as it can, because every pair made is two people playing instead of waiting. When several pairings make equally many matches, it prefers the one that gets the people who have waited longest into a game. Whoever is not paired stays in the lobby for the next snapshot. {{region_rule}}
sections.problem: Implement match_lobby(players, max_gap). Each player is (player_id, region, skill, wait_ms). Two players can be paired if they are in the same region and abs(skill_a - skill_b) <= max_gap[region]; each player is in at most one pair. Choose the pairing that (1) makes the most pairs and, among those, (2) has the largest total wait_ms of the paired players. Return (pairs, left): the number of pairs, and the ids of the players left in the lobby, sorted ascending. All wait_ms values are distinct, which makes the set of players left unique; who plays whom may not be unique, so it is not returned.
sections.constraints: Up to 150 001 players in the timing check, with skills between 1 000 and 3 000, so thousands of players are inside any one player's gap. Expected: O(n log n) time, a sort followed by one linear pass. Searching for partners pair by pair, or scanning every earlier player in the gap for each player, is far too slow.
sections.assumptions: Skills, waits, regions and gaps are hypothetical. Real matchmakers also weigh rating uncertainty, network latency, parties and windows that widen with time; this snapshot rule is the exercise's own.
sections.criteria: Same-region pairs only, inclusive gap; the number of pairs maximised before the wait; ties broken by the total wait of the paired players; the uncrossing argument that justifies working in skill order; O(n log n) with a deque or another monotone structure, not a scan of the gap per player; left list sorted; empty and single-player lobbies; can discuss widening gaps, groups and starvation across snapshots.

clarifications.q: Is a skill gap exactly equal to max_gap allowed?
clarifications.a: Yes. The gap must be at most max_gap.

clarifications.q: Should the longest-waiting player always be paired first?
clarifications.a: Only if that does not cost a pair. The number of pairs comes first; the total wait of the paired players only breaks ties.

clarifications.q: With max_gap 0, can two players with the same skill play?
clarifications.a: Yes.

clarifications.q: Do I return who plays whom?
clarifications.a: No. Several pairings can be equally good; the set of players left waiting is unique, so return that.

clarifications.q: Can players from different regions be paired?
clarifications.a: Never.

hints: Sort a region's players by skill. If a ≤ b ≤ c ≤ d (by skill) are paired as (a, c) and (b, d), or as (a, d) and (b, c), then (a, b) and (c, d) are allowed too. So some best pairing pairs players who are next to each other among the paired players, in skill order.

Scanning in skill order, each player therefore either stays, or plays one earlier player j while everyone between j and them stays. Let best[i] be the best (pairs, total paired wait) over the first i players.
best[i + 1] = max(best[i], best[j] + (1, wait[j] + wait[i])) over the j inside the gap. Those j form a window that only slides forward, so a monotonic deque gives the maximum in O(1) amortised.
Python compares tuples lexicographically, which is exactly "pairs first, then wait". Record each player's choice so you can walk back and collect who stayed.
followups: Why does pairing neighbours greedily from the lowest skill already maximise the number of pairs, and why does it not settle who is left waiting?
Each player's allowed gap widens the longer they wait. Does the sorted structure survive, and what breaks?
Groups of two must play another group of two (2v2), with the gap measured between the groups' average skills. How does the problem change?
Snapshots run every two seconds. How would you stop the same player being left out snapshot after snapshot, and how would you measure it from logs?

rules.ask: How many possible pairings does a lobby of 150 000 players have? What does sorting by skill let you skip?
Skills 10, 20, 30 with a gap of 10: pairing from the lowest skill pairs (10, 20). When is that the wrong player to leave waiting?
Players at skill 0, 20, 21 and 41 with a gap of 20, and the player at 21 has waited longest. Who do they play under your rule, and how many pairs do you make?
General matching works but costs far more than n log n. What property of "skill gap at most D" lets you avoid it?
Why can you drop a candidate from the back of your deque, and why does the front only ever move forward?

templates.title: Spreadsheet selections: distinct cells under overlapping ranges
templates.subtopic: A1 reference parsing, bijective base 26, coordinate compression, union area of rectangles

sections.scenario: A spreadsheet app's status bar shows how many cells the current selection covers. People build selections from many ranges (Ctrl-click, or a saved list of references), and the ranges often overlap. A sheet has 1,048,576 rows and 16,384 columns (A to XFD), so one selection can cover billions of cells; the count has to be exact and instant, which rules out visiting cells. {{forms_rule}}
sections.problem: Implement cells_selected(selections). selections is a list of A1-style reference strings. Return the number of distinct cells covered by at least one of them. Column letters are bijective base 26 (A = 1, …, Z = 26, AA = 27, …, XFD = 16 384); rows are numbered from 1. {{extra_rule}}
sections.constraints: Up to 2 000 selections in the timing check, many covering millions of cells. Letters are upper case and there are no spaces or sheet names. Expected: O(n log n) with a sweep and a segment tree, or O(n²) after compressing the coordinates. Anything proportional to the number of cells is far too slow.
sections.assumptions: The grid size and the reference forms follow the publicly documented conventions of common spreadsheet apps (check current docs); the selections are hypothetical. Sheet names, named ranges, R1C1 notation and hidden rows are out of scope.
sections.criteria: Bijective base-26 columns; inclusive rectangles; overlaps counted once; corners in any order, whole columns and whole rows (Hard+); $ markers, several areas per selection and the -1 sentinel (Very Hard); an exact union by compression and a sweep, never per-cell work; arbitrary-precision counts; can discuss double coverage, sums over sparse values and incremental updates.

clarifications.q: Is B2:D10 the same as D10:B2?
clarifications.a: Yes. A range is the rectangle spanned by its two corners, in whatever order they are written.

clarifications.q: What does C:E cover?
clarifications.a: Every row of columns C to E: 3 × 1,048,576 cells.

clarifications.q: A cell is in three selections.
clarifications.a: It counts once.

clarifications.q: How large can the answer be?
clarifications.a: The whole sheet is 17,179,869,184 cells, more than 32 bits; Python integers are fine.

clarifications.q: What if a reference is off the grid?
clarifications.a: Return -1. This only occurs at the hardest level; otherwise every reference is valid.

hints: Parse every reference into an inclusive rectangle (c1, c2, r1, r2) first. Whole columns are rows 1 to 1,048,576; whole rows are columns 1 to 16,384.
Only the edges matter: the distinct values of c1 and c2 + 1 cut the sheet into column strips inside which the set of covering rectangles does not change.

Sweep the strips from left to right. In each, the covered rows are the union of the active rectangles' row intervals: sort and merge them, or keep a segment tree over the compressed row boundaries with a cover count per node.
followups: The status bar should also show how many cells are covered by two or more selections. What changes in your sweep?
The status bar also shows the SUM of the selected values, and only a few million cells are non-empty. How would you add them up without double counting overlaps?
The user drags one range's corner 60 times a second. How would you update the count incrementally instead of recomputing it?
Co-authors each have their own selection in a shared workbook. How would you count the cells selected by anyone, on a service holding thousands of open workbooks?

rules.ask: How many cells does A:XFD cover, and how long does your loop take to visit them?
With 2 000 overlapping ranges, how many intersection terms does inclusion–exclusion need?
What column numbers does your conversion give for AA and XFD? Is this ordinary base 26, and where does it differ?
A compressed grid has up to (2n)² cells. At 2 000 selections, how many is that, and can you avoid building it?
When a node is fully covered by a rectangle, what is its covered length, and what happens to it when that rectangle ends?

templates.title: Signature scan — every occurrence of many byte patterns in one pass
templates.subtopic: multi-pattern matching (Aho–Corasick), overlapping and nested matches, streamed chunks

sections.scenario: Desktop operating systems ship with built-in anti-malware protection, and one of the oldest techniques it can use is to look for known byte sequences, called signatures, inside files. This exercise imagines a much simplified signature stage. A signature set of many thousands of entries is updated several times a day. For every file it is given, the stage must report every place where any signature occurs. A later stage, which is not part of this exercise, weighs those occurrences together with other evidence. A missed occurrence is a missed detection, and a slow scan is felt by every user of the machine.
sections.problem: Implement scan(signatures, chunks). signatures is a list of (sig_id, pattern) pairs, and each pattern is a non-empty bytes. chunks is a list of bytes, the file's contents in the order they were read. Return a list of (offset, sig_id) for every occurrence of every signature in the whole file, which is the chunks one after another. offset is the position of the occurrence's first byte, counted from 0 at the start of the file. Occurrences may overlap, including two occurrences of the same signature. Sort the list by offset, then by sig_id. Return an empty list if nothing occurs. {{nesting_rule}} {{chunk_rule}}
sections.constraints: Up to 20 000 signatures of up to 64 bytes each, and files of up to 500 000 bytes in this exercise. Any byte value can appear. Something close to O(n + m + z) is expected for n file bytes, m total signature bytes and z occurrences. Searching the file once per signature is 20 000 passes and is not fast enough. Do not join the chunks into one buffer: a real file can be far larger than memory, so keep only what you need between chunks.
sections.assumptions: The signatures, files and sizes are hypothetical, and real anti-malware engines use far more than exact byte signatures. Signatures are exact bytes with no wildcards. sig_id values are unique strings.
sections.criteria: Every occurrence reported, overlaps and nested signatures included, with identical patterns reported under each id; offsets counted from the start of the file across chunks; correct ordering and an empty list when nothing matches; one automaton built once, with failure links built breadth-first and outputs merged or linked; state carried between chunks without joining them; a clear O(n + m + z) argument; sensible answers on updates, wildcards, prefilters and memory layout.

clarifications.q: Do overlapping occurrences count separately?
clarifications.a: Yes. 00 00 occurs twice in 00 00 00, at offsets 0 and 1.

clarifications.q: Can one signature's bytes appear inside another's, or can two signatures have identical bytes?
clarifications.a: In general, yes, and each id is reported on its own. Ties at one offset are ordered by sig_id.

clarifications.q: What is the offset of an occurrence that starts in one chunk and ends in the next?
clarifications.a: The position of its first byte in the whole file.

clarifications.q: Does the signature set change during a scan?
clarifications.a: No. It changes a few times a day, so building an index once per update and then scanning many files with it is the expected shape.

clarifications.q: Can a chunk be empty?
clarifications.a: Yes. An empty chunk changes nothing.

hints: Put every signature into one trie. Walking the file through the trie finds the signatures that start where the walk started. What should a mismatch do, so that the walk never moves backwards in the file?
Give every trie node a failure link to the node for the longest proper suffix of its string that is also in the trie. Compute the links breadth-first, so a node's parent already has its link.

One node can complete several signatures: its own, and every signature that is a suffix of its string. Merge outputs along failure links when you build, or keep a link to the nearest node with an output, so you never walk the whole chain on every byte.
The automaton's current state is the only thing a scan needs to carry from one chunk to the next.
followups: The signature set is updated several times a day. What do you rebuild, how long does it take for 20 000 signatures, and how does a scan already in progress switch to the new set?
Signatures gain wildcards: "any byte here", or "a gap of 0 to 8 bytes". How do you keep a single pass over the file, and what do you verify afterwards?
Most files contain no signature at all. How would you make that common case cheaper, and how would you show that your shortcut never misses an occurrence?

The scanner runs on millions of machines, and memory per process matters more than build time. How would you lay out the automaton (dicts, a dense 256-wide table, a compressed table), and what does each cost?

rules.ask: How many passes over the file is that with 20 000 signatures, and roughly how long does it take on a 500 KB file?
Does finditer report two overlapping occurrences, or two signatures at the same offset? What does a 20 000-way alternation cost per byte in a backtracking regex engine?
How many distinct signature lengths can there be, how many hash lookups per file byte does that make, and what do you do on a hash collision?
The next file is 6 GB. What do you keep between chunks instead of the whole file?
One signature is a suffix of a longer one. When the scan completes the long one, how do you report the short one too, without walking every failure link on every byte?

templates.title: Cheapest storage tier schedule for a blob, with early-deletion minimums
templates.subtopic: day-by-day states with a capped counter, early-deletion charges, tie-breaking

sections.scenario: Cloud object storage offers access tiers for blobs. Hotter tiers cost more to store and less to read. Cooler tiers cost less to store and more to read, and an archive tier is offline: a blob there must be brought back online (rehydrated) before it can be read. Cooler tiers also have a minimum stay: a blob that leaves them early is charged for the remaining days. A storage-cost team wants to judge its automatic lifecycle rules. For a sample of blobs it replays each blob's daily read trace and computes, in hindsight, the cheapest possible tier schedule. That cost is the lower bound every rule is measured against.
sections.problem:
Implement cheapest_tiering(reads, tiers). reads[d] is the number of reads of the blob on day d, for D = len(reads) days, and D ≥ 1. tiers maps a tier name to {"store", "read", "min_days", "enter", "leave"}. The rules of this exercise are:

  1. On every day the blob is in exactly one tier. On day 0 it is uploaded into any tier, with no fee.
  2. A day in tier t costs store + reads[d] × read. A tier whose read is None is offline: the blob cannot be in it on a day with reads[d] > 0.
  3. A move from tier s on day d − 1 to a different tier t on day d costs leave of s plus enter of t, and counts as one tier change.
  4. A stay is a run of consecutive days in one tier. When a stay of k days in tier s ends with k < min_days of s, it costs an extra (min_days − k) × store of s, the early-deletion charge. This applies whether the stay ends with a move or with the deletion in rule 5.
  5. After the last day the blob is deleted. Rule 4 applies to the final stay, and no leave fee is charged.

Return (total_cost, changes) for the cheapest schedule. If several schedules cost the same, return the one with the fewest tier changes. {{tier_rule}}
sections.constraints: Up to 3 650 days (ten years) and four tiers in this exercise, with min_days up to 180. At least one tier is online, so a schedule always exists. All prices are non-negative integers. Something close to O(D · Σ min_days) is expected. Enumerating tier sequences is Tᴰ. Trying every start day of every stay is O(D² · T²) and is too slow at ten years.
sections.assumptions: All prices, minimums and traces are hypothetical. Prices are already for this blob's size, in integer micro-units per day or per read. Public cloud object stores publish their own tiers, minimum stays and early-deletion rules, and the rules here are this exercise's simplified version: check current docs before using them for anything real. Rehydration is instant in this exercise. Reads are known for the whole trace, because this is a replay.
sections.criteria: Correct (cost, changes) with the fewest changes on a cost tie; early-deletion charges at both moves and the final deletion, with no leave fee at deletion and none at an exact-minimum stay; offline tiers excluded on days with reads; free initial placement; a day-by-day programme over (tier, capped days) with the move cost computed once per tier per day; integer arithmetic; a clear complexity argument; credible answers on lifecycle rules, fleet evaluation and rehydration delay.

clarifications.q: Is the upload on day 0 charged an enter fee?
clarifications.a: No. The blob can start in any tier for free. Only later moves pay leave and enter.

clarifications.q: Does deleting the blob after the last day pay the leave fee?
clarifications.a: No. It pays only the early-deletion charge of the final stay, if that stay is shorter than its tier's minimum.

clarifications.q: If the blob goes hot → cool → hot → cool, does each cool stay count separately against the minimum?
clarifications.a: Yes. Each stay is counted from the day the blob enters the tier.

clarifications.q: Can the blob sit in the archive between two days with reads?
clarifications.a: Yes, if that is cheaper. It pays the archive's leave fee, which models rehydration, when it comes back online.

clarifications.q: What if two schedules tie on cost and on changes?
clarifications.a: The answer is only the pair (total_cost, changes), so it is the same either way.

hints: Write a schedule's cost as a sum over days plus a charge when each stay ends. What do you need to know about the current stay to price its end?
Only the number of days in the current tier matters, and only up to that tier's minimum: after min_days days the stay owes nothing more. So a state is (tier, min(days in tier, min_days)).
A move into tier t on day d only needs, for each other tier, the cheapest way to end a stay there on day d − 1, including its early-deletion charge and leave fee. Compute that once per tier per day.
Compare (cost, changes) as a pair, or pack it into one integer such as cost << 20 | changes, so a single comparison orders both.
followups: In production the reads are not known in advance. Propose a lifecycle rule, for example "move to cool after N days without a read", and explain how you would use this function to choose N.
Millions of blobs follow one rule. How would you evaluate a candidate rule across the fleet without replaying every blob, and what bias could your sample introduce?
Rehydration actually takes hours, so a read on day d needs the blob online from day d − 1. What changes in your programme?
Prices change on a known day in the middle of the trace. What changes in your states, and which price should an early-deletion charge use? State the rule you would choose and why.

rules.ask: How many schedules are there for 3 650 days and four tiers? Estimate how long enumerating them would take.
Give a trace where choosing the cheapest tier for each day on its own is not the cheapest schedule. What do the minimum stay and the move fees do to a per-day choice?
Python's default recursion limit is about 1 000 frames. What happens on a 3 650-day trace, and how would you turn your recursion into a loop?
How many (start, end) pairs is that for ten years of days, times how many tier pairs, and how long will it take in Python?
Where could a float sneak into your compared or packed costs, and how do you keep the answer an exact integer?

templates.title: Debug the meeting attendance report
templates.subtopic: sessions per device, interval union, time zones, identity keys

sections.scenario: Organisers of online meetings in a collaboration suite can download an attendance report: one row per attendee with when they first joined, when they last left and how long they were present. Organisers have raised several complaints about one report generator. People who dropped out and rejoined appear to have arrived late. Someone on a laptop and a phone at once shows 90 minutes in a 60-minute meeting. A late-evening meeting shows negative durations. An organiser on the west coast of North America sees join times seven or eight hours ahead of the clock on the wall. All the external guests appear as a single person called "guest". The generator below is the suspect.
sections.problem:
Fix attendance_report(meeting, events) so that it meets this specification. {{replay_rule}}

  1. Input. meeting is {"id", "start", "end", "tz_offset_min"}. events is a list of {"ts", "type", "user", "name", "device"} in time order. Every ts is in Unix seconds (UTC), and type is "join" or "leave".
  2. Attendee. An attendee is identified by user. A guest has user set to None and is identified by "guest:" + name.
  3. Sessions. A join opens a session for that attendee on that device. The next leave for the same attendee and device closes it. A leave with no open session is ignored. A device never joins twice without leaving. A session still open when the events end closes at meeting["end"].
  4. Time present. seconds is the total length of the union of the attendee's sessions over all devices. Time on two devices at once counts once, and the gap between leaving and rejoining does not count.
  5. Times shown. first_join is the attendee's earliest join and last_leave is the latest end of any of their sessions. Both are shown in the organiser's local time, which is UTC plus tz_offset_min minutes, as "YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM", with the seconds dropped.
  6. Output. {attendee: {"first_join", "last_leave", "seconds"}}, with an entry for every attendee who has at least one session.
sections.constraints: Keep the function's shape and output format. Up to 200 000 events in one meeting, processed in O(n log n) time.
sections.assumptions: Event shapes, offsets and volumes are hypothetical and simplified. The organiser's offset is fixed for the whole meeting, so there is no daylight-saving change during it. Each event is delivered once, in time order. Every join is at or after meeting["start"].
sections.criteria: Finds and explains every bug with its user-visible symptom; first join kept across rejoins; time on several devices merged as a union; durations computed on absolute timestamps, not clock times; times shown in the organiser's offset, including a date that rolls over; guests keyed by name and kept apart from members; the fix stays minimal and O(n log n); adds a test per bug.

clarifications.q: Two guests have the same display name. Are they one attendee?
clarifications.a: In this exercise, yes. The report has nothing else to tell them apart. A guest and a member with the same name are always different attendees.

clarifications.q: Does the gap between leaving and rejoining count as time present?
clarifications.a: No. Only time inside a session counts.

clarifications.q: If someone is connected on a laptop and a phone at the same time, is that time counted twice?
clarifications.a: No. Count the union once.

clarifications.q: How are seconds dropped from the times shown?
clarifications.a: Round down: 09:14:59 is shown as 09:14.

clarifications.q: How many bugs are there?
clarifications.a: Several, of different kinds. The checks point at each one.

hints: Write out the expected row for one person who joins at 09:00, leaves at 09:10, rejoins at 09:30 and leaves at 09:50. Then compare it with what the code reports.
What is 00:10 minus 23:50 when both are measured in seconds since midnight?
Sort one attendee's sessions by start and merge the ones that overlap before adding up their lengths.
Which key does a guest get, and which key does the second guest get?
followups: Organisers want the report while the meeting is still running. What changes in how you store open sessions and compute seconds?
Events from several regions arrive late and out of order after an outage. Which parts of your fix still hold, and what would you change?
Organisers ask for a flag "present for at least 75% of the meeting". Is the denominator the scheduled length or the actual one, and what happens for people who joined from two devices?
Some organisations hide user names in usage reports. How would you keep guests distinct in the report without showing their names?

rules.ask: A person is on a laptop and a phone for the same 30 minutes. What does your total say, and what should it say?
What duration does your arithmetic give for a session from 23:50 to 00:10?
The specification gives one fixed offset for the meeting. When would a named time zone give a different answer, and which should the report use?
Two different guests are both called "Alex". What does your key do, and what would you need from the meeting service to tell them apart?
After an outage, events arrive out of order. Does your first-join logic still hold?

templates.title: Assistant usage reporting for tenant admins, without retaining prompt content
templates.subtopic: privacy-preserving usage telemetry, exact distinct users over rolling periods, pseudonymous reporting

sections.scenario: A productivity suite includes an AI assistant inside {{apps}} apps: documents, spreadsheets, email, meetings, chat and others. The suite's admin centre already offers usage reports for its apps, with an option to conceal user names. Tenant admins now want the same for the assistant: actions per app, active users, and adoption trends over the last {{periods}}, so they can decide where to extend licences and where to train people. About {{tenants}} tenants generate {{daily_actions}} assistant actions a day. The prompts people type and the responses they get are customer content. The reporting pipeline must never store them, not even for a day.
sections.problem: Design the pipeline from the client's usage event to the admin's report. Cover the event schema and how you keep content out of it, ingestion and deduplication, what makes a user "active", exact active-user counts per period, per-app and per-day aggregates, adoption trends against licensed users, the report's day boundary, concealed names, breakdowns by department with a minimum group size of {{min_group}} users, deletion of users who leave a tenant, data residency for tenants that require their data to stay in a geography, and how a metric definition change is restated.
sections.constraints: No prompt text, response text, file names or titles, or any other field derived from content, anywhere in the pipeline, including logs and error queues. Active-user counts must be exact per tenant, because admins compare them with licence counts. Reports are refreshed daily and may be up to two days behind. A user removed from the tenant's directory is removed from reports within 30 days in this exercise. One tenant can never see another tenant's data.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, periods, thresholds and windows are hypothetical. Clients emit one event per assistant action with the tenant id, the user's directory object id, the app, an action type from a fixed list, an outcome, the client version and a timestamp. Licence assignments come from a daily directory export per tenant. Department comes from the directory too.
sections.criteria: An allow-listed event schema enforced at the edge, with content excluded from storage, logs and error queues; event ids and deduplication; a clear active-user definition; exact distinct users per period from a per-user activity table, not summed daily counts; licence-aware adoption; stable per-tenant pseudonyms and serving-time concealment; small-group suppression that also protects against subtraction; deletion within 30 days across every table; residency respected; versioned metric definitions with restatements; a plan for each incident.

clarifications.q: What counts as an active user?
clarifications.a: A licensed user who performed at least one intentional assistant action in the period: a prompt submitted, a suggestion accepted, a summary generated. Opening the assistant's pane does not count.

clarifications.q: Which day boundary does a report use?
clarifications.a: UTC days in this exercise, and the report says so. Explain what you would do if admins asked for their own time zone.

clarifications.q: Can I keep prompt text for a few days for debugging?
clarifications.a: No. Not in this pipeline and not temporarily. Quality work on the assistant is a separate, governed process outside this design.

clarifications.q: Do admins see individual users?
clarifications.a: Yes, per-user rows are part of the report, unless the tenant turns on concealed names. Then users appear under pseudonyms that stay stable across the tenant's reports.

clarifications.q: Can I sum daily active users to get 30-day active users?
clarifications.a: No. A person active on 20 days would be counted 20 times.

hints: Write the event schema first, as an allow-list. Every field that is not on the list is dropped at the edge, before anything is stored.
Distinct users over 180 days cannot be summed from daily counts. Which small per-user table lets you answer every period exactly?
Decide where concealment and small-group suppression are applied, in storage or when serving, and justify it against the deletion requirement.
followups: A client release starts sending a free-text error detail that sometimes contains a fragment of the user's prompt. How do you detect it, and what do you do about data already stored?
An admin asks for adoption by department, and one department has three users. What do you show, and how do you stop the hidden number being worked out from totals?
The definition of active changes: accepting a suggestion inside a document now counts. How do you restate history, and what do admins see?
A tenant's data has to move to another geography in the middle of a quarter. What happens to its history and its reports?
Product asks for cross-tenant benchmarks such as "tenants of your size". What can you publish, and what must you never publish?

rules.ask: An admin sees 30-day active users 1% above the number of licences. How do you explain that, and where in your design do you need exact counts?
A malformed event lands in your error queue with its raw payload. What could be in that payload, and who can read it?
The same hashed user id appears in every tenant's report. What can someone link with it, and how would you key or salt the hash?
A user is removed from the directory. Which of your tables still hold their identifier, and how do you remove it within 30 days?
An admin in a tenant at UTC+13 sees Monday's usage split across two report days. What do you change, or how do you explain it?

incidents: A client release ships an error field that, for one day, carries fragments of prompt text in about 0.1% of {{daily_actions}} events.
A directory sync failure marks every user in 300 tenants as unlicensed for a day, and their adoption charts drop to zero.
One department in a large tenant has fewer than {{min_group}} users, and its numbers can be derived by subtracting the other departments from the tenant total.

templates.title: Daily cloud resource inventory with change history from activity events
templates.subtopic: state reconstruction from events and snapshots, identity across moves, validity intervals

listing: a full listing once a day
a full listing once a week

sections.scenario: A platform team runs a public cloud estate of {{subscriptions}} subscriptions and about {{resources}} resources. Every control-plane operation, such as a create, an update, a delete or a move, produces an activity event: about {{daily_events}} a day. In this exercise the activity log keeps events for {{log_retention}}. The team can also take {{listing}} of every resource through the cloud's resource API. Finance, security and compliance all ask versions of the same questions: what existed at the end of a given day, with which tags, location and size; who changed a resource and when; and which cost belongs to which team, even after resources were moved.
sections.problem: Design the pipeline that builds a daily inventory and a change history from the activity events and the listings. Cover the sources and how each lands, the identity of a resource when its identifier changes, how an event that names an operation becomes a change in state, missed and late events, reconciliation against listings, deletions that cascade from a resource group to its contents, the history model and the daily inventory built from it, reruns and backfills, and how users can tell an observed change from an inferred one.
sections.constraints: The inventory for any past day must be reproducible. Events can be hours late, and some changes produce no event that reaches you. A listing takes hours to run, so it is not a single instant. Every change in the history must say whether it was observed in an event or inferred from a listing. Resource identifiers are case-insensitive.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, windows and schedules are hypothetical. An event carries an event id, the operation, the resource id, the caller, a status (started, succeeded or failed) and a timestamp. It does not carry the resource's properties after the change. In this exercise a move or a rename changes the resource id, and its event lists the old and the new id; check current docs for how a real cloud behaves. Deleting a resource group deletes everything in it, and in this exercise the contents may not each produce their own event.
sections.criteria: Raw events and listings landed immutably with event-id deduplication; a surrogate resource key with an id-history table that survives moves and renames; succeeded operations turned into state changes, with properties read after the fact; validity-interval history with observed and inferred changes marked; reconciliation that infers missed creates and deletes from listings, with honest timestamps; cascade deletes handled; late events inserted correctly; reproducible daily inventories; case-insensitive identity; a plan for each incident.

clarifications.q: Does an event tell me the resource's new tags or size?
clarifications.a: No. It tells you which operation ran on which id, by whom, when, and whether it succeeded. The resulting properties come from reading the resource, or from the next listing.

clarifications.q: What does a move look like?
clarifications.a: One succeeded event with the old id and the new id. The new id has a different resource group or subscription in its path.

clarifications.q: Do failed operations appear?
clarifications.a: Yes, with status failed. Only succeeded operations change state, and one operation can appear as started and then succeeded.

clarifications.q: How complete is a listing?
clarifications.a: Complete for every subscription the team can read, but it runs for hours, so two resources in it may have been read hours apart.

clarifications.q: Are ids compared case-sensitively?
clarifications.a: No. The same resource can appear with different capitalisation in different sources.

hints: Separate a resource's identity from its current id string. Give it a surrogate key, and keep a history of the id strings it has had.
Treat an event as evidence that something changed and when, and a listing as the truth at the time each resource was read. Record the source of every change.
Store history as validity intervals. The inventory for a day is then a query for the versions valid at the end of that day.
followups: A listing shows 2 000 resources that no event ever mentioned. What do you write into the history, and with which timestamps?
A resource group with 500 resources is deleted, and you receive one event. What happens to the inventory and the history?
A resource moves to another subscription and its id changes. Cost records for the month are keyed by the id. How do you join cost to the inventory across the move?
The pipeline was down for longer than the activity log's {{log_retention}}. How do you rebuild, and what do you mark as unknown?
Auditors ask who changed a tag, and the change was made by an automated policy, not a person. What does your history show?

rules.ask: A move changes the id string. What does your primary key do, and how does the history follow the resource?
The listing takes four hours. A resource created and deleted during it appears in neither listing. Does that matter, and which source catches it?
A late event arrives for a change that happened before a listing already recorded the newer state. How do you insert it into intervals that are already closed?
If you overwrite the current state, how do you answer "what existed on the 3rd of last month"?
You normalise ids to lower case for joins. What do you show to users, and could two different resources ever collide?

incidents: The event feed stalls for six hours. The next listing ({{listing}}) brings thousands of inferred changes with no caller, and security asks who made them.
A reorganisation moves 400 resource groups to new subscriptions overnight. The next morning, cost allocated to the affected teams drops by a third because cost records use the new ids.
A tagging policy rewrites a tag on every resource in {{subscriptions}} subscriptions within an hour, and the event volume is twenty times the usual {{daily_events}} a day rate for that hour.

templates.title: Recurring meeting series — occurrences, exceptions, and attendance on the right instance
templates.subtopic: recurrence rules, occurrence identity, exceptions, series splits, time zones

sections.scenario: A workplace suite schedules meetings in its calendar and runs them as online meetings. About {{daily_occurrences}} meeting occurrences happen a day, and about {{series_share}} of them belong to a recurring series: daily stand-ups, weekly one-to-ones, a monthly review on the second Tuesday. An organiser defines a series in their own time zone, and many attendees live in {{dst_regions}}, where clocks change on different dates. Single occurrences are moved, cancelled or given a different agenda and attendee list; an organiser can also edit "this and all following occurrences", and a series can have no end date. In this exercise every occurrence of a series shares one online join link. Each online occurrence produces join and leave events per participant, and some produce a recording and a transcript. People want attendance per occurrence, no-show rates for one-to-ones, the recording of "last Tuesday's review", and how many meeting hours a person had last week.
sections.problem: Design the data model for series and their occurrences, and for what happens in them. Cover: the series and its recurrence rule (with the time zone it is defined in); the identity of one occurrence, stable when it is moved; exceptions (modified and cancelled occurrences); how a "this and following" edit splits a series without losing the history of the past occurrences; how and how far ahead occurrences are materialised for a series with no end ({{horizon_months}} months in this exercise); how join and leave events and recordings are attributed to an occurrence when every occurrence shares one join link; and the facts with their grains that answer the questions above.
sections.constraints: An occurrence keeps its identity when its time changes, so attendance, chat and recordings stay attached to it. A recurring meeting's wall-clock time stays fixed in the organiser's time zone across daylight-saving changes. The calendar's state on a past date must be reconstructable (what the series said last month, before an edit). Join and leave events arrive at least once and can be late by hours from clients that were offline.
sections.assumptions: Volumes, shares, regions and the horizon are hypothetical. Recurrence rules follow the familiar iCalendar ideas (a rule, a start, a time zone, exception dates, and a recurrence id for each instance, its original start); you can say "RRULE" and "RECURRENCE-ID" and be understood. The meeting service gives each participant session a session id. People outside the tenant (guests) can join.
sections.criteria: Series, exceptions and materialised occurrences kept apart; a stable occurrence key (series and original start in the series' zone) that survives moves; wall-clock rules with the time zone stored, expanded per occurrence; "this and following" as a split that freezes the past and links both halves; a materialisation horizon with incremental extension and exceptions applied on arrival; an explicit join attribution rule with a grace window and an unmatched bucket; at-least-once events deduplicated by session id; facts at stated grains (occurrence, participant session); each incident contained, corrected and guarded.

clarifications.q: Is a moved occurrence a new meeting?
clarifications.a: No. It is the same occurrence with a new start. Its identity is the series plus its original start, which never changes.

clarifications.q: How do I know which occurrence a join belongs to if the link is shared?
clarifications.a: In this exercise the join event carries only the meeting's join link and a timestamp. You decide the attribution rule and say what happens to someone who joins early, or stays past the end.

clarifications.q: What does "this and following" do to the past?
clarifications.a: The organiser expects past occurrences, their attendance and recordings to be unchanged, and future ones to follow the new rule.

clarifications.q: Which time zone is a series in?
clarifications.a: The organiser's, chosen when the series is created. Attendees see it in their own zones.

clarifications.q: Does a cancelled occurrence count as a no-show?
clarifications.a: No. A cancelled occurrence has no expected attendees.

hints: Keep three things apart: the rule (series), the exceptions to it (keyed by original start), and the materialised occurrences you report on.
An occurrence key of (series id, original start in the series' time zone) survives moves; a key built from the actual start does not.

Attribute a join to the occurrence whose scheduled window (with a grace period either side) contains the join time, using the occurrence's actual start after any move, and record when no occurrence matched.
followups: Walk a weekly 09:00 series in an organiser's zone across a daylight-saving change in {{dst_regions}}. What is stored, and what does an attendee in another zone see the week the clocks change?
The organiser moves next week's occurrence from Tuesday to Wednesday, then edits "this and all following" to Thursdays starting the week after. Show the rows that exist afterwards.
Two occurrences of a daily series both fall inside your grace window for one join (one ran late, the next was moved earlier). Which one gets the join, and how is that visible?
A series has no end. How far do you materialise, how do you extend the horizon, and what does "meeting hours next quarter" mean beyond {{horizon_months}} months?
At {{daily_occurrences}} occurrences a day, which tables are keyed and partitioned how, and what does a late exception (a cancellation entered after the occurrence was materialised) cost to apply?

rules.ask: The organiser moves an occurrence by an hour after three people accepted it. If the occurrence key includes the start time, what happens to the acceptances and to the recording link?
You stored occurrences in UTC. A series is 09:00 in the organiser's zone; the clocks change next month. Which rows change, and who changes them?
An occurrence was materialised, then cancelled as an exception a week later. How does your expansion apply that, and what did yesterday's report say?
Someone joins 20 minutes early for a daily stand-up and stays through the next day's occurrence slot by mistake. How many occurrences did they attend?
After the split, how does a report of "this one-to-one's attendance for the year" find both halves?

incidents: The week clocks changed in {{dst_regions}}, recurring occurrences in the affected zones (series are about {{series_share}} of all meetings) were an hour off in the warehouse because they had been expanded once with a fixed UTC offset; joins fell outside every occurrence window and the no-show rate for one-to-ones doubled.

An organiser's "this and all following" edit on a two-year weekly series re-keyed every past occurrence; their attendance and recordings now point at occurrence ids that no longer exist, and the series shows twice in the yearly report.
Cancellations entered after the nightly materialisation of the next {{horizon_months}} months were not applied until the next full rebuild; cancelled occurrences showed as 100% no-shows for a week.

templates.title: Device fleet updates — builds, rings, offers, install states and rollbacks over time
templates.subtopic: device identity, ring assignment history, install state machines, as-of build

sections.scenario: An operating system ships a quality update every month and a feature update less often. Organisations that manage their devices put each device in an update ring (here: {{rings}}), and each ring sets a deferral: a quality update is offered to a device in a ring only once the ring's deferral has passed (for example {{deferral_days}} days). About {{devices}} devices report to the update service. A device moves through states for each update: offered, downloading, downloaded, installing, pending restart, installed, or failed with an error code; an installed update can be removed again, by a person or by an automatic rollback when the device fails to start, which happens to about {{rollback_share}} of installs for some builds. Devices separately send an inventory heartbeat with their current OS build. Devices can be offline for weeks, are reimaged, renamed, moved between rings, and occasionally move to another organisation. Admins and release teams ask: what share of each ring is on the latest build N days after release, how long from offer to installed, the failure rate by build and error code, and which devices were on build X on a given date.
sections.problem: Design the data model. Cover: device identity (what survives a reimage, a rename and a hardware repair, and what does not); the ring assignment history and the ring's own settings over time; the build catalogue (version, build and revision numbers, quality versus feature updates, which build supersedes which); offers; install attempts and their state events; how you derive a device's installed build at any past time when heartbeats and install events disagree; and the facts and grains that answer the four questions, including what "on the latest build" means for a device that has been offline since before the release.
sections.constraints: State events are delivered at least once, out of order, and stamped by device clocks that can be wrong by days; the service also stamps when it received each event. A device's build can go down (rollback). The ring a device was in, and the ring's deferral, must be known as of any past date. An admin sees only their organisation's devices.
sections.assumptions: Device counts, ring names, deferrals and rollback shares are hypothetical. Each device has a service-issued device id and a hardware id; a reimage issues a new device id in this exercise unless the device is re-registered with the same hardware id. Error codes are opaque strings.
sections.criteria: Device identity defined against reimage, rename and resale; ring membership and ring settings each versioned; a build catalogue with an order so cumulative updates and rollbacks compare correctly; install attempts as state machines with idempotent, order-tolerant events (device and received times kept); a derived build-interval history reconciling heartbeats and events; "on latest build" defined with offline devices shown apart; facts at stated grains with tenant-level access; each incident contained, corrected and guarded.

clarifications.q: Which source is the truth for the current build, heartbeats or install events?
clarifications.a: Neither alone. Heartbeats are periodic and say what is running; install events say what happened. You decide how to combine them and what wins when they disagree.

clarifications.q: Can a device skip a monthly update?
clarifications.a: Yes. Quality updates are cumulative, so a device that was offline installs only the latest one.

clarifications.q: Does an offline device count in "share on the latest build"?
clarifications.a: You decide, and say so. Admins want to see offline devices separately rather than as failures.

clarifications.q: Can a ring's deferral change?
clarifications.a: Yes. An admin can shorten it for an urgent fix or pause updates for the ring; past offers were made under the old setting.

clarifications.q: What is a rollback in data terms?
clarifications.a: An event that removes an installed update, after which the device runs the previous build.

hints: Separate desired state (ring, its settings, the offer), attempts (install attempt with its state events) and observed state (heartbeats). The device's build history is derived from attempts and observations.
A cumulative update makes "latest build" a comparison on the build order, not a match on one update id.
Keep device time and received time on every event; order by the device's own sequence number when there is one, and never trust the device clock alone for the order of events.
followups: Write the state machine for one install attempt. Which transitions are legal, which event wins when two arrive out of order, and how do you store it?
A device installed the update, rolled back two days later, and was offered it again. Show its build history rows and how the "share on latest build" for that week counts it.
A device is reimaged and re-registers with the same hardware id. Which history is joined, and which is not?
An admin shortened the ring's deferral from {{deferral_days}} days to zero for one update. How does your model show which offers were early and why?
At {{devices}} devices with daily heartbeats, what is stored at full grain, for how long, and what is kept as daily snapshots or intervals?

rules.ask: A support ticket asks which build this device was on last Tuesday at 10:00, before a rollback. With a current-build column, can you answer?
The heartbeat says build 2 while an install-succeeded event for build 3 arrived an hour later with an earlier device timestamp. What is the device on, and when did it change?
A device's clock was a week behind. Its events land in last week's partitions. What does that do to "time from offer to installed", and how do you detect it?
A refurbished device is sold to another organisation with the same hardware id. Whose history does it carry, and who may see it?
What exactly is versioned: the device's ring, the ring's settings, or both? Which one decides whether an offer was on time?

incidents: A month after a feature update, {{rollback_share}} of devices had rolled back automatically, but the release dashboard still counted them on the new build because "install succeeded" events were never superseded by the later removal.

An admin shortened a ring's deferral from {{deferral_days}} days to zero for an urgent fix. The ring settings table kept only the current value, so the compliance check flagged every earlier offer in that ring as late.

After a mass reimage at a large organisation, its devices re-registered with new device ids; the fleet appeared to grow, ring coverage halved overnight, and every device's install history started again.

templates.title: Cloud resource hierarchy — management groups, subscriptions, resource groups and tags over time
templates.subtopic: changing hierarchies, closure tables, as-of rollups, tag history

sections.scenario: Customers of a public cloud organise what they run in a hierarchy: a tree of management groups (here up to {{mg_depth}} levels below the root), subscriptions that each sit in exactly one management group, resource groups inside a subscription, and resources inside a resource group. Policies and access assignments made at any level apply to everything below it. Tags (name and value pairs) can be set on subscriptions, resource groups and resources; in this exercise a resource does not inherit tags from its resource group or subscription unless the organisation's own rule copies them. A large customer platform team reports across {{subscriptions}} subscriptions and {{resources}} resources: monthly cost by department (a management group) and by cost-center tag, policy scope ("which resources did this assignment cover on the 3rd"), and missing-owner reports. Subscriptions move between management groups when departments reorganise; resources move between resource groups and subscriptions; tags on about {{tag_change_share}} of resources change on a given day.
sections.problem: Design the data model for the hierarchy, its changes and its tags. Cover: how the management-group tree is stored and versioned (adjacency, path or closure table, with validity intervals); how subscriptions, resource groups and resources are placed in it over time; a stable identity for a resource whose id path changes when it moves (in this exercise a move changes the resource's id; check current docs); tag history and the "effective tag" rule you choose (own tag, else resource group's, else subscription's); and the rollups: cost by management group as the hierarchy was on the usage date versus as it is today, cost by effective tag, and the resources an assignment at a given scope covered on a date.
sections.constraints: Hierarchy changes are rare but questions about the past are frequent and must give the same answer every time they are asked. Cost already invoiced to departments is not silently re-allocated when the tree changes. Tag names are treated case-insensitively and values case-sensitively in this exercise (check current docs). A resource's cost history must follow it across moves.
sections.assumptions: Counts, depth and change rates are hypothetical. Cost arrives daily per resource id and meter, and can be restated for a few days. The platform team receives hierarchy and tag changes as activity events plus a daily full snapshot; events can be missed, and the snapshot is the tiebreaker.
sections.criteria: A hierarchy with validity intervals (closure or path table) and as-of rollups; both allocation rules defined, with invoiced months closed and changes shown as restatements; stable surrogate resource keys across moves; tags as rows with history, a stated precedence rule and case handling; change compaction for no-op rewrites; snapshot-versus-event reconciliation with corrections recorded; policy scope answerable as of a date; each incident contained, corrected and guarded.

clarifications.q: Should a department's cost follow today's hierarchy or the one on the usage date?
clarifications.a: Both are requested. Finance wants usage-date allocation for invoices; leadership wants today's structure for trends. Say which is the default and how the other is produced.

clarifications.q: Can a management group move under another one?
clarifications.a: Yes, with all its children. Depth stays within {{mg_depth}} levels in this exercise.

clarifications.q: When a resource moves, is it a new resource?
clarifications.a: Its id changes in this exercise, but the platform team wants one continuous history.

clarifications.q: Who sets the tags?
clarifications.a: Owners, deployment pipelines and a remediation policy that writes missing tags. All three can set the same tag on the same day.

clarifications.q: Are deleted resources kept?
clarifications.a: Their history is: past cost and past scope still need them.

hints: A closure table (ancestor, descendant, depth) with valid-from and valid-to answers "everything under this group on date D" with one join; rebuilding it on each tree change is cheap because the tree is small.
Give each resource a surrogate key and a mapping from every id path it ever had to that key, with intervals.
Store tags as rows (scope, name, value, valid from, valid to) rather than columns; derive effective tags per resource per day with your precedence rule.
followups: A management group with 300 subscriptions moves under a different parent on the 15th. Show the closure rows that change and what the month's cost by department looks like under each allocation rule.
A resource moves from one subscription to another and its id changes. How does its cost history appear in each department's report for that month?
Write the "effective cost-center tag on date D" rule as a query sketch. What happens to cost when the tag is added on the 20th: is the first half of the month untagged or re-labelled?
Tags change on {{tag_change_share}} of resources a day, mostly by automation rewriting the same value. How do you keep tag history small without losing real changes?
The activity events missed a subscription move that the daily snapshot shows. What do you write, with which validity, and how do downstream reports learn of the correction?

rules.ask: The report needs every resource under one top-level group, as of each day of the month. How many recursive walks is that, and what would you precompute instead?
Finance invoiced a department last month. A subscription moves out today. What does your rebuilt report now say last month cost them?
The resource moved and its id changed. Which key do the cost rows join to, and how do the two ids become one history?
An owner adds a new tag name that ten teams then misspell in different cases. What happens to your table, and how do reports group them?
The snapshot and the events disagree about when a move happened. Which do you trust for the validity interval, and how is that recorded?

incidents: A subscription with heavy spend moved to another management group mid-month. The chargeback report, rebuilt nightly from the current tree, moved the whole month's spend to the new department after invoices had been sent.

A tag remediation policy rewrote the cost-center tag on every resource it covered in one night; the tag history recorded each rewrite as a change, the tag table tripled, and "tag changes per day", normally about {{tag_change_share}}, spiked to 60%.
Resources moved between subscriptions in a clean-up got new ids; the cost report showed each as deleted and a new resource created, and their month split across two departments.

templates.title: Game entitlements — what a player could play on a date, and why
templates.subtopic: entitlement intervals, rotating catalogues, sharing rights, precedence

sections.scenario: A games platform serves about {{players}} players on consoles, PC and cloud streaming. A player can own a game (a purchase, a code redemption, a bundle) and its add-ons; they can also hold a subscription in one of several tiers, each giving access to a rotating catalogue of about {{catalogue_titles}} titles. Titles join the catalogue on a date and leave on a date announced {{leave_notice_days}} days ahead, and a title can be in one tier, on one platform or in one region and not another. Subscribers can buy a catalogue title at a member discount, and then keep it when it leaves. Subscriptions lapse when a payment fails and resume later; purchases can be refunded. In this exercise a player can share their purchased games with a family group of up to {{family_size}} members under the platform's sharing rule, and a subscription's catalogue is not shared. Support agents need to answer "could this player play this title on this date, and through which right?"; the content team wants hours played per title split by right (owned, subscription, shared), and publishers are paid partly on subscription play.
sections.problem: Design the entitlement model. Cover: the product catalogue (titles, editions, add-ons that require a base game, platforms); licence grants and revocations from purchases, redemptions and refunds; subscriptions with their periods, tier changes, lapses and resumes; catalogue availability windows by tier, platform and region; sharing grants that derive from another player's licences; a derived "access interval" per player, title and right; the precedence rule when several rights apply at once; and how play sessions are attributed to one right for the content and publisher reports.
sections.constraints: "Could they play it on date D" must give the same answer later, even after the catalogue changes or a refund. A play session is attributed to exactly one right. A refund revokes the licence and everything derived from it from the refund time, not retroactively. Regions and platforms are part of every availability rule.
sections.assumptions: Player counts, catalogue size, notice period and family size are hypothetical, and so are the sharing and tier rules described here; they are this exercise's rules, not a statement of any current product policy. Play sessions arrive from clients with a session id and can be uploaded late from offline consoles.
sections.criteria: Immutable sources (orders, refunds, subscription periods, catalogue windows, sharing memberships) with derived access intervals; subscription access as the intersection of membership and catalogue windows by tier, platform and region; add-on dependency on a base right; refunds and owner changes propagating to derived sharing rights from the right time; one stated precedence rule so each session gets exactly one right; time zones and region boundaries explicit; closed reporting periods restated, not rewritten; sizing and refresh strategy; each incident contained, corrected and guarded.

clarifications.q: If a player owns a title and it is also in their subscription, which right does play count against?
clarifications.a: You choose the precedence and state it; publishers care because subscription play may be paid differently from owned play.

clarifications.q: Does an add-on bought for a catalogue title still work after the title leaves the catalogue?
clarifications.a: The add-on licence remains, but in this exercise it needs a base-game right to be playable.

clarifications.q: What happens when a subscription lapses for three days and resumes?
clarifications.a: No catalogue access during the gap. Saved games are out of scope.

clarifications.q: Is a member-discount purchase different from a normal purchase?
clarifications.a: It is a normal perpetual licence once bought; record the discount and the subscription that made it possible.

clarifications.q: Can a shared game be played if the owner's account is banned or the purchase refunded?
clarifications.a: No. Sharing rights end when the owner's licence does.

hints: Model rights as intervals: (player, title, right type, source id, valid from, valid to, platform, region). Every question becomes an interval lookup.
Derive the intervals from immutable sources (orders, refunds, subscription periods, catalogue windows, sharing memberships) so they can be rebuilt; never edit an interval by hand.
A subscription right is the intersection of the player's subscription interval with the title's catalogue window for that tier, platform and region.
followups: A player subscribes, plays a catalogue title, buys it at a member discount in its last {{leave_notice_days}} days, and the title then leaves. Show the access intervals and how each play session is attributed.
The owner of a family of {{family_size}} refunds a game a month after buying it. Which intervals close, from when, and what happens to the hours already played by the family?
A title leaves the catalogue at midnight. Midnight where? Show how regions and the session that started before midnight are handled.
