A player upgrades to a higher tier mid-period, then downgrades. Which titles were available on each day, and what does the support agent see?
At {{players}} players, how large is the access-interval table, how is it partitioned and refreshed, and which questions do you answer from sources instead of intervals?

rules.ask: A support agent asks whether the player could play the title last March. Your table says they own it now. Did they then, and through which right?
The title left the catalogue last month and its row was deleted. How do you now answer whether a subscriber could play it on the 10th of last month?
The refund came after the family played for 40 hours. Are those hours re-attributed, and what does the publisher report for that month say?
The player owns the base game through sharing and has the title in their subscription. Which right wins for attribution, and does the answer change if the sharing owner is refunded tomorrow?
The catalogue window is defined per region. A session that started at 23:30 local continues past the leave time. Is it allowed, and how is it counted?

incidents: A nightly clean-up deleted catalogue rows for titles that had left; support could no longer say whether a subscriber could play a title last month, and the publisher report for a closed month changed on a rebuild.

Play-time attribution counted sessions twice for players who bought a title at a member discount during its last {{leave_notice_days}} days in the catalogue: their sessions matched both the subscription right and the new licence.
A refund revoked the buyer's licence, but sharing intervals derived from it stayed open; a family of {{family_size}} kept playing for weeks and that play was reported as owned.

templates.title: Policy compliance by day — carrying the latest evaluation forward
templates.subtopic: as-of latest row, carry-forward across days, lifetimes, half-open days

sections.scenario: A cloud governance team assigns policies to the resources of a subscription (here {{policy_list}}) and wants a daily compliance trend per policy. The policy engine evaluates a resource when it is created or changed and on a periodic scan, and writes one row per evaluation to policy_evaluations; between evaluations nothing is written, so a resource can go days without a new row while its last state still stands. Resources are created and deleted over time and are listed in resources. {{lifecycle_rule}} evaluation_id is unique and assigned by the ingestion pipeline; it is not in time order.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns day, policy_id, assessed_resources, compliant, non_compliant, compliance_pct for every UTC day from {{start_day}} to {{end_day}} inclusive ({{days}} days). For a day D and a policy, a resource counts if it still exists at the end of D (its deleted_at is NULL or at or after the next midnight) and it has at least one evaluation for that policy made before the next midnight (evaluated_at < D + 1 day). Its state that day is its latest such evaluation, carried forward from earlier days when it was not re-evaluated on D. {{state_rule}} assessed_resources = compliant + non_compliant; compliance_pct is ROUND(100.0 * compliant / assessed_resources, 1). Return one row per day and policy with at least one assessed resource, ordered by day, policy_id.
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). Days are half-open in UTC: an evaluation exactly at midnight belongs to the new day, and a resource deleted exactly at midnight existed for the whole of the day before. The sample has {{resource_rows}} resource rows and {{evaluation_rows}} evaluations; production has hundreds of millions of evaluations a day across many subscriptions.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical schema, policy names, resource names and states. Evaluations are never written for a resource outside its lifetime. The report covers one subscription, so there is no tenant column.
sections.criteria: A calendar of days joined to evaluations before each day's end; latest evaluation per resource, policy and day by evaluated_at (ties as stated), carried forward; existence at the end of the day with half-open boundaries; at Hard and above, exempt chosen as the latest state and then excluded, and ties by evaluation_id; at Very Hard, evaluations attached to the lifetime they fall in so a re-created resource starts with no state; correct rounding and deterministic ordering; can explain a state-change interval table, staleness and the denominator.

clarifications.q: Does a resource evaluated before the first reported day count on that day?
clarifications.a: Yes. Its latest evaluation before the next midnight is its state, however old.

clarifications.q: A resource was created on D but not evaluated until D + 1. Does it count on D?
clarifications.a: No. It has no state yet for any policy.

clarifications.q: Do evaluations after {{end_day}} matter?
clarifications.a: No. They are after the end of every reported day.

clarifications.q: What if the latest evaluation is for a different policy?
clarifications.a: Each policy has its own state for a resource; take the latest per resource and policy.

clarifications.q: Should days with no new evaluations at all still appear?
clarifications.a: Yes, if any resource still has a carried-forward state for the policy.

hints: Build the calendar of days with generate_series, then join each day to every evaluation made before its end.
DISTINCT ON (day, policy_id, resource_id …) … ORDER BY …, evaluated_at DESC, evaluation_id DESC keeps the latest evaluation per resource, policy and day.
Decide whether a resource exists at the end of the day after picking its latest state, using the lifetime the evaluation belongs to.
followups: This query re-reads every evaluation for every day. At hundreds of millions of evaluations a day, what would you store instead so the daily trend is cheap (a state-change interval table, or a daily snapshot), and how is it kept correct?
The engine sometimes re-evaluates a resource and writes the same state again. How would you compute the number of real state changes per policy and day?
The dashboard shows 92% compliant. Which resources are not in the denominator at all, and should the dashboard say so?
A resource's state is three weeks old because the periodic scan skipped it. How would you flag stale states, and should they still count?

rules.ask: evaluation_id is assigned on ingestion and is not in time order. Which evaluation does MAX(evaluation_id) pick for a resource scanned late, and what should decide "latest"?
An evaluation at exactly 00:00:00 changes a resource's state. Which day does your expression give it, and which day's row does it change?
Your window picks the latest row per resource overall. How does a day in the middle of the range see the state the resource had on that day, not today's?
A resource is deleted at exactly midnight. Show the comparison you wrote and the two days around the deletion.
The latest evaluation is exempt but the one before was non-compliant. Did you filter exempt rows before or after picking the latest, and what does each give?

incidents: A version of this report that counted only each day's evaluations showed compliance swinging between 40% and 95% day to day across {{policy_list}}: the periodic scan covered a different set of resources each day, and resources not scanned that day dropped out of the denominator.
After a clean-up deleted hundreds of resources, the trend still counted them as non-compliant for weeks, because the query ignored deleted_at and carried their last state forward.

templates.title: Staged OS update rollout with automatic safeguard holds
templates.subtopic: rollout control, cohort health signals, automatic holds

sections.scenario: A desktop operating system ships a new feature update to about {{devices}} eligible devices. Devices are not all alike: the combination of device model, firmware, drivers and installed security or management software forms about {{cohorts}} distinct hardware and software cohorts. Consumers receive the update when the vendor offers it; organisations place their managed devices in their own deployment rings (a pilot ring first, broad rings after a deferral of some days), and the vendor's offer applies within those choices. The vendor releases the update in {{stages}} stages, each offered to a larger share of eligible devices. Devices that opted in to diagnostic data report install outcomes (downloaded, installed, failed with an error code, rolled back), boot failures and crash rates after install. When a cohort shows a problem, the vendor places a hold: in this exercise's rule, a hold stops offering the update to every device matching a rule (for example "this device model with this driver version") until a fix ships, and is then released.
sections.problem: Design the rollout system: the offer decision a device receives when it checks for updates; how stages widen; the health-signal pipeline from device reports to per-cohort metrics; automatic detection of a cohort that is failing; creating, matching and releasing holds; how organisations' ring choices are respected; and the audit trail that explains why any one device was or was not offered the update on a given day. Say how a stage widens only after {{decision_window}} of healthy signals.
sections.constraints: An update check from a device must be answered in under 200 ms p99, and devices check at all hours. A hold must reach every matching device's next check within 15 minutes of being created. A device that has already installed the update is not uninstalled automatically; it can be offered a fix or a rollback. Diagnostic data comes only from devices whose users allowed it, so some cohorts are thinly observed. Every offer decision must be reproducible later.
sections.assumptions: All device counts, cohort counts, stage counts and timings are hypothetical. Devices send their model, firmware, driver and software inventory with each update check. Install outcomes arrive minutes to hours after the event; devices that are offline report days later.
sections.criteria: Control plane and data plane separated, with versioned, audited rules compiled for fast evaluation; a deterministic, stable assignment of devices to stages that represents cohorts; an evaluation order that respects organisations' rings and holds; a health pipeline that compares against a baseline, accounts for late reports and small samples, and fails closed when its own data is late; holds as specific attribute rules that can be narrowed and released safely; offer decisions reproducible per device and day; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Who defines the cohorts?
clarifications.a: You do. Say which attributes form a cohort, and what happens when a problem depends on an attribute your cohort key leaves out.

clarifications.q: Does a hold cancel downloads already in progress?
clarifications.a: In this exercise a device that has downloaded but not installed re-checks the hold before installing; a device that has installed is handled by a fix or a rollback offer.

clarifications.q: Can an organisation override a hold?
clarifications.a: In this exercise an administrator can explicitly install on managed devices despite a hold, and the system records that choice; consumers cannot.

clarifications.q: How many devices must report before a cohort is judged?
clarifications.a: That is part of your design. Some cohorts have a few hundred devices in total.

clarifications.q: Who releases a hold?
clarifications.a: An engineer, when the fix (a driver update, an app update or a revised OS update) is available; you decide how much of that is automated.

hints: Separate the control plane (stages, holds, ring policies, versioned and audited) from the data plane that answers device checks from a compiled, cached copy of the rules.
Health is a comparison, not an absolute: compare a cohort's failure rate on the new update with the same cohort's rate on the previous update, and require a minimum sample before acting.
A hold is a rule that matches device attributes. Decide how specific it is, and what happens to devices whose attributes change after the hold is placed.
followups: Walk through one update check: what the device sends, what the service evaluates, in what order (eligibility, organisation ring, holds, stage), and what it returns.
How do you decide that a cohort with 300 devices in stage one is failing, without placing holds on hundreds of healthy cohorts by chance?
A problem appears only for one driver version on several device models. How does the detection find the common attribute, and how is the hold scoped?
How do you widen from stage to stage automatically, and what stops the widening when the health signal itself is late?
An organisation asks why 40 of its devices did not receive the update last Tuesday. What does the system let you show them?

rules.ask: The stage is a percentage of devices. How do you keep the same device in the same stage across checks, and keep each stage representative of every cohort?
A cohort has 40 reporting devices and 3 failures. Is that over your threshold? How does the rule behave for small and large cohorts?
A new hold is created. How long until every cached copy of the rules has it, and what does a device checking in the meantime receive?
Devices that installed before the hold keep failing to boot. What does your system offer them, and how do you know it worked?
Install outcomes arrive hours late from devices that were offline. How does your per-cohort metric avoid judging a cohort before its failures have arrived?

incidents: Midway through stage two, a hardware partner releases a new graphics driver. Devices with that driver and the new update fail to boot, but the automatic hold rule is keyed on device model only, so no hold matches; failures rise across 60 models at once.
The health-signal pipeline falls 10 hours behind over a weekend. The rollout controller reads the empty window as "no failures" and widens to the next of the {{stages}} stages.

A hold for one device model is released when the fixed driver ships, but the release removes the hold for the whole model, including devices still on the old driver; they are offered the update and fail.
In stage one, detection places holds on more than a thousand small cohorts in a day, most of them healthy, because a few failures among a few dozen devices crossed a fixed percentage threshold.

templates.title: Presence across many clients for a collaboration app
templates.subtopic: multi-device aggregation, fan-out, connection management

sections.scenario: A workplace chat, meetings and calling app shows each person's presence next to their name: Available, Busy, In a call, In a meeting, Do not disturb, Away, Offline, and a status the person sets themselves, optionally until a time. A person is often signed in on several clients at once (desktop, web, phone), and their presence is derived from all of them plus their calendar: activity or idleness on each client, joining a call on any client, a meeting in the calendar, a status they set. At peak about {{online}} people are online, served from {{regions}} regions. Each person's presence is watched by about {{watchers}} others on average (people viewing a chat, a channel, a contact list or a meeting roster), and far more for some. Clients keep a connection to the service and send a heartbeat every {{heartbeat}} seconds.
sections.problem: Design the presence service: the per-client signals and how they are stored; the rule that combines a person's clients, calendar and set status into one presence; detection that a client is gone; subscriptions (who is watching whom) and fan-out of changes to watchers; how it spans {{regions}} regions; and the privacy controls (an organisation can limit what people outside it see). Say how a change reaches watchers quickly without flapping.
sections.constraints: A presence change should reach online watchers within 2 seconds p99. A person whose every client has disconnected must show Offline within a bounded time you state. Presence must never show a person as available while they are in a call on any client. A status set "until 17:00" must end at 17:00 in the person's time zone even if none of their clients is running. Watchers outside the person's organisation may see only what the organisation allows.
sections.assumptions: All counts, rates and intervals are hypothetical. Calendar events arrive from the calendar service as change notifications. Each client sends events with a sequence number per connection.
sections.criteria: Per-client leases renewed by heartbeat and a stated offline bound; presence as a deterministic function of client states, calendar and set status with explicit precedence (a call outranks idleness); server-side timers for expiries; change suppression and coalescing before fan-out; subscriptions scoped to active views, with special handling for very large audiences; a home-region or replicated design with its costs across regions; organisation-level visibility rules applied on read; reconnect storms absorbed with jitter and grace periods; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Which signal wins when clients disagree?
clarifications.a: You define the precedence; say why. A call on any client and a set status are the usual candidates to outrank idleness.

clarifications.q: Does every watcher need every change?
clarifications.a: Only watchers currently looking at the person. A contact list in a closed window needs nothing until it opens.

clarifications.q: Is presence stored for analysis later?
clarifications.a: Not in this exercise; it is live state. Say what you would keep for debugging.

clarifications.q: Are people in different regions watching each other?
clarifications.a: Yes, often, especially across organisations and in large meetings.

clarifications.q: Can a phone app keep a connection open in the background?
clarifications.a: Not reliably; mobile operating systems suspend background apps, and push notifications are the usual channel.

hints: Keep per-client state with a lease that heartbeats renew; a person's presence is a pure function of their live client states, calendar and set status, recomputed when any of them changes.
Fan-out cost is changes per second × watchers per change. Reduce both: suppress changes that do not change the visible state, and push only to watchers with an active view.
Put a person's presence state in one home region and route reads and subscriptions to it, or replicate it; each choice has a cost when people in different regions watch each other.
followups: Write the precedence rule that combines three clients, a calendar meeting and a set status into one presence. What happens when the phone stops heartbeating mid-call?
How many fan-out messages per second does your design send at peak, and what do you do for a person watched by 50,000 people in a company-wide meeting?
A person goes idle on the desktop and immediately active on the phone. How do you avoid sending Away then Available to every watcher?
A region loses its connection gateways for a minute and every client reconnects at once. What do watchers see, and how does the service survive the reconnect?
How does a set status expire at 17:00 local time when none of the person's clients is connected?

rules.ask: At {{online}} people and a {{heartbeat}}-second heartbeat, how many writes per second is that, and which of them change anything a watcher can see?
Who subscribes to a person's channel, and what happens to the cost when a meeting roster of 10,000 people all watch each other?
Two clients of the same person send updates whose clocks disagree by a minute. Whose update wins in your design, and is that the right presence?
A watcher in one region looks at a person homed in another. What latency does each read or update take, and what does a region failure do to that person's presence?
The phone cannot keep a connection in the background. How does the service know whether the phone is still in a call?

incidents: A gateway deployment in one of the {{regions}} regions restarts its connection servers at once; millions of clients reconnect within seconds, each reconnect publishes Offline then Available, and fan-out traffic rises fortyfold for ten minutes.
People in calls on their phones show Away: the phone's client is suspended in the background and stops sending activity, and the precedence rule lets the desktop's idle state win over the call.
Statuses set "until 17:00" stay on all night for people who closed every client before 17:00, because expiry is evaluated only when a client sends an event.

A company-wide meeting with 60,000 attendees makes every attendee watch every other on the roster; fan-out for that tenant saturates its partition and presence for unrelated people on the same partition lags by minutes.

templates.title: Permission-aware document index for a workplace assistant
templates.subtopic: security trimming, permission change propagation, deletion

sections.scenario: A productivity suite adds an assistant that answers employees' questions using their organisation's documents: files in team sites and personal storage, pages and shared notebooks. The index covers about {{documents}} documents across {{tenants}} customer organisations (tenants). Who may open a document is decided by the suite's own permissions: users and groups (groups can contain groups, and the largest has about {{largest_group}} members), permissions inherited from a site or folder unless a document breaks inheritance, and sharing links (specific people, or anyone in the organisation who has the link). The assistant retrieves passages relevant to the question and answers from them. It must use only content the asking user can open at the moment they ask, and a permission change, a removal from a group or a deletion must take effect in the assistant within {{apply_within}}.
sections.problem: Design the indexing and retrieval system: ingestion of content changes and permission changes; chunking and embeddings; the index layout across tenants; how permissions are represented next to indexed passages; security trimming at query time; the propagation of permission changes, group changes and deletions; and caching that never leaks content between users. Say how retrieval quality survives trimming when most of the closest passages belong to documents the user cannot open.
sections.constraints: Retrieval must answer in under 300 ms p95 including trimming. No passage from a document the user cannot open may reach the model, the answer, a citation or a cache another user can read. Tenants' data never mixes in one result. A deleted document's passages and embeddings must be gone from the index within {{apply_within}}. Re-embedding a document costs model compute; say how often it happens.
sections.assumptions: All counts, latencies and limits are hypothetical. The suite's storage service emits change notifications for content, permissions and deletions; the directory service emits group membership changes. Both can be replayed from a point in time.
sections.criteria: Per-tenant index isolation; passages carry unexpanded access principals with query-time expansion of the user's memberships; security trimming inside the search with a recall-preserving fallback, plus a final check of the few chosen documents against the source of truth; permission, group and deletion changes as an ordered change stream with a measured propagation lag and alerts against the target; deletion covering every copy (indexes, embeddings, caches); caches keyed by the user's effective permissions or not shared; audit records proving which documents were used; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Can we copy the full permission list onto every passage?
clarifications.a: You can; say what happens when a group of {{largest_group}} people gains access to a site with a million passages, and when one person leaves that group.

clarifications.q: Is the permission check done by the storage service at query time?
clarifications.a: It can answer "can this user open these documents?" for a batch of up to a few hundred documents in about 50 ms. You decide whether and when to call it.

clarifications.q: Does a sharing link for "anyone in the organisation with the link" let everyone in the organisation see the document in the assistant?
clarifications.a: In this exercise, no: only people who have opened the link are treated as having access. Say how you learn who they are.

clarifications.q: Are answers cached?
clarifications.a: You may cache retrieval or answers, if you can prove the cache cannot serve one user's content to another.

clarifications.q: What does a user see when nothing they can open is relevant?
clarifications.a: The assistant says it found nothing it can use; it must not hint that restricted content exists.

hints: Store on each passage the access principals at the level they were granted (groups, not expanded members), and expand the user's own group memberships at query time. A group change then updates one membership, not millions of passages.
Trimming after retrieving the top k passages loses recall when most of them are filtered out. Filter inside the search, or retrieve more and fall back to a second pass.
Treat the index's permission data as a cache of the source of truth, and verify the final few documents against the storage service before they reach the model.
followups: Walk through one question: from the user's identity to the passages the model sees. Where is each permission check, and what does each one cost?
A person is removed from a group that grants access to a site with 2 million passages. What changes in your index, and how long until the assistant stops using that site for them?
Most of the 50 closest passages to a question belong to a document the user cannot open. How does your retrieval still find the best passages they can open?
A document is deleted. List every place its content can still exist in your system, and how each is cleaned within {{apply_within}}.
How would you prove to a customer's security team that the assistant never used content the user could not open?

rules.ask: The top 50 passages all come from one document the user cannot open. What does your system return, and how do you know?
A group of {{largest_group}} people gains access to a site with a million passages. How many index updates does flattening cost, and how long do they take?
Two people in the same tenant ask the same question but can open different documents. What is your cache key, and what happens when one of them loses access an hour later?
Your filter is a list of principals per passage. Does your vector index support filtering during search, and how does recall change when the filter is very selective?
A person is removed from a group at 10:00 and asks a question at 10:20. Does your nightly job meet the {{apply_within}} requirement?

incidents: An administrator removes 4,000 people from a group that grants access to a finance site. The index flattened group members onto every passage, so the change is applied by rewriting millions of passages; for six hours, longer than the {{apply_within}} target, removed people still get answers quoting the budget.
A user asks about a project they work on and the assistant says it found nothing: the 50 closest passages all came from a restricted planning document, and trimming them left an empty list.
An answer cache keyed by tenant and question text serves one person's answer, citing a document shared only with them, to a colleague who asks the same question.
A document deleted from a team site still appears in citations for two days, because its passages were removed from the main index but not from a smaller index built for recently changed content.

templates.title: Game achievements from consoles, PC and cloud play
templates.subtopic: offline sync, idempotency, tamper resistance, aggregate counts

sections.scenario: A gaming network serves about {{players}} monthly players on consoles, PCs and cloud streaming. Each of its {{titles}} games defines achievements with points: some unlock on a single event ("finish the tutorial"), others track progress ("win 100 matches"). The game reports unlocks and progress to the network. Players can play offline on a console or PC for up to {{offline_days}} days; the device queues achievement events and sends them when it reconnects. The same account plays on several devices, sometimes at the same time. The network shows each player's unlocked achievements with unlock dates, their total points, a feed of friends' unlocks, and for each achievement the share of a game's players who have unlocked it ("rarity"). Events peak at {{peak_events}} per second, much higher on a big game's launch day.
sections.problem: Design the achievements service: the event contract between games and the network; ingestion from online and offline devices; per-player achievement state and progress; total points; rarity per achievement; the friends feed; and defences against duplicated, replayed and tampered events. Say what the source of truth is and which views are derived.
sections.constraints: An achievement unlocks at most once per player; its unlock date is when it was earned, not when the event arrived. Total points must equal the sum of unlocked achievements' points at all times a player looks. Progress never moves backwards. A player sees their own unlock within 5 seconds when online. Rarity may lag by an hour. Unlocks found to be fraudulent can be revoked, and every view must reflect the revocation.
sections.assumptions: All player counts, title counts and rates are hypothetical. Games run on the device; PC games can be modified by players. Each event carries a player id, title id, achievement id or progress value, a device id, a device sequence number and a device timestamp, and is signed by the device's runtime.
sections.criteria: An event contract with stable ids and signed events; an unlock ledger keyed by (player, title, achievement) with conditional inserts as the single source of truth; progress merged monotonically; earned time chosen with plausibility checks; projections (points, feed, rarity) derived idempotently from the ledger and rebuildable; a hot-key strategy for rarity; tamper detection with revocation that propagates to every projection; offline sync bounded by device sequence numbers; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Can a game change its achievements after release?
clarifications.a: A publisher can add achievements in an update; in this exercise, points of an existing achievement never change, and an achievement is never deleted, only hidden.

clarifications.q: Which device's timestamp counts when two devices report the same unlock?
clarifications.a: You decide, and say what you show if the earliest claim is implausible.

clarifications.q: Is progress reported as increments or as a total?
clarifications.a: As the game's current total for that player; you decide what to do when two devices report different totals.

clarifications.q: How is rarity's denominator defined?
clarifications.a: You define it: for example, players who have launched the game at least once.

clarifications.q: What makes an event suspicious?
clarifications.a: Signs include unlocks faster than the game allows, impossible order, a signature that does not verify, or a device seen sending events for many accounts.

hints: Make the ledger of accepted unlocks the source of truth, keyed by (player, title, achievement), with a conditional insert; points, feeds and rarity are projections of it.
Progress reported as a total can be merged with max, which is idempotent and order-independent across devices.
Rarity is a count per achievement divided by players per title; counting each unlock once with a hot counter per popular achievement needs sharding or periodic recomputation.
followups: A console reconnects after {{offline_days}} days with 180 queued events, some for achievements the player already unlocked on PC since. Walk through what is accepted, what is ignored, and which unlock date is kept.
On a big game's launch day, one achievement is unlocked by 3 million players in an hour. What happens to your rarity counter and the friends feed?
How do you keep total points correct when an unlock is revoked as fraudulent?
A modified PC client sends unlock events for every achievement of a game in one second. How is it detected, and what do other players' rarity figures show meanwhile?
How would you rebuild every player's state for one game if a bug accepted bad events for a week?

rules.ask: A device retries the same unlock three times after timeouts. Does your counter count it three times? What is the idempotency key?
The player's console clock is set two years in the past. Which unlock date do you show, and how do you decide it is implausible?
Exactly once between which two points? The device queues events offline for {{offline_days}} days and may send some twice after a crash.
Ranking was not asked for. What would it add to your storage and write path, and is it worth it here?
You partition by player. Where does the per-achievement rarity count live, and what happens to it on launch day?

incidents: On a big game's launch day, "finish the tutorial" is unlocked by millions of players within an hour; the single counter row for its rarity becomes the slowest write in the system and unlock confirmations back up for every game.

A console reconnects after {{offline_days}} days offline and sends 200 queued events; 40 of them are for achievements already unlocked on PC, and a bug in the total-points projection adds their points again.
A modified PC client publishes unlocks for every achievement of a new game within one second for thousands of accounts; the rarest achievement shows as unlocked by 12% of players by morning.
A game update ships with a progress bug that reports zero for "win 100 matches" after a reinstall; players' progress bars reset.

templates.title: OS reliability analytics — crash rates, bucketing and preview-build regressions
templates.subtopic: rate denominators, crash bucketing, regression detection

sections.scenario: A desktop operating system publishes preview builds to about {{preview_devices}} enrolled devices, {{builds_per_week}} times a week, before the changes reach general release. Opted-in devices send crash and hang reports: the process or kernel component that failed, the faulting module and its version, an exception code and a stack of addresses, plus the device's build, model and driver set. About {{reports}} reports arrive per day across preview and released builds. To save bandwidth, after a device sends the first report for a given failure on a day, it uploads further reports for it at {{upload_rate}}. Devices also send a daily usage heartbeat saying which build they ran and for how long. Engineering teams want crash rates per build, per component and per device model, crashes grouped into buckets so that one bug is one bucket, and an alert when a new preview build is less reliable than the one before it.
sections.problem: Design the reliability analytics platform: ingestion of reports and heartbeats; symbolisation of stacks; bucketing; the crash-rate metrics (define numerator and denominator precisely); comparing a new build with the previous one; routing a regression to its owning team; and what is kept, for how long. Say how the metric for a build published this morning becomes trustworthy, and when.
sections.constraints: A regression on a new preview build should be detected within 24 hours of release where enough devices run it. Bucket identities must stay stable across builds, so a bug's history follows it. Reports are pseudonymous (a device id, no user identity) and raw stacks are kept for 30 days; aggregates may be kept longer. Devices that update first are not a random sample of the population.
sections.assumptions: All device counts, report volumes, rates and retention periods are hypothetical. Symbol files for each build are published to a symbol store by the build system. Reports and heartbeats can arrive days late from devices that were offline.
sections.criteria: Precise rate definitions with exposure denominators (device-days or usage hours) and crashing-devices as the robust primary metric; throttled reports estimated correctly; symbolisation as a retried stage with reprocessing; bucket keys from symbolised frames that survive rebuilds, with merge and split operations; regression detection that compares like with like, requires minimum exposure and reports uncertainty; late-arriving heartbeats handled by completeness watermarks; cohort analysis that finds model and driver interactions; ownership routing with a fallback; retention by tier; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Is the metric crashes per device-day or crashing devices per device-day?
clarifications.a: Both are used; define each and say which one drives regression alerts, and why.

clarifications.q: How are throttled reports counted?
clarifications.a: The first report of a failure per device per day is always sent; later ones are sampled at {{upload_rate}}. Say how you estimate totals.

clarifications.q: Who owns a bucket?
clarifications.a: The team that owns the faulting module, from a module ownership list that is mostly but not entirely up to date.

clarifications.q: Should the new build be compared with the previous preview build or with the released build?
clarifications.a: Both are useful; say which question each answers.

clarifications.q: Can you see which devices installed which drivers?
clarifications.a: Yes, from the inventory each device sends with its heartbeat.

hints: The denominator is exposure: device-days (or usage hours) on that build, from heartbeats. A rate with crashes from reports and devices from installs counts the wrong thing.
A bucket key built from module names and function names (after symbolisation) survives a rebuild; one built from raw addresses or offsets does not.
Compare like with like: the same devices on the old and new build, or the new build's population re-weighted to the old one's mix of models and drivers.
followups: Define the crash rate you alert on: numerator, denominator, grain, and how throttled reports and late heartbeats enter it.
What is your bucketing key, and what happens to it when a module is recompiled and every offset changes?
A build released this morning has 40,000 device-days by evening. How do you decide whether its crash rate is worse than the previous build's, and with what confidence?
The new build's early devices are mostly newer hardware. How does that bias the comparison, and how do you correct it?
A crash appears only with one driver version on one device model. How does the platform surface that combination without testing every pair?

rules.ask: One device in a crash loop sends 2,000 reports in a day. What does that do to your metric, and is that what engineers need to know?
A module is recompiled and every address in it moves. Does your hash put the same bug in a new bucket?
The new build has 900 device-days so far and 3 crashes in a component that had 1 the day before. Is that a regression? How does your rule decide?
Heartbeats for today's device-days arrive over the next three days. What does your real-time rate show at 09:00 for a build released at 06:00?
Reports after the first are uploaded at {{upload_rate}}. How do you estimate the total, and which metric does the sampling not affect?

incidents: The symbol store is unavailable for a day after a build is published; that day's reports cannot be symbolised, land in hundreds of new "unknown" buckets, and the build's existing buckets look healthier than they are.

A preview build recompiles a common module; the bucketing key includes the faulting offset, so every crash in that module opens a new bucket, and the regression detector reports 300 "new" crashes in one morning.
A new build's crash rate looks 40% worse than the previous build's in its first day; most of its first devices are a new hardware model whose graphics driver crashes on every build.

Reports reach the platform hours before the same day's heartbeats do, so the crash rate for each new build starts very high every morning and falls through the day; owners have learned to ignore morning alerts.

templates.title: A consent-setting change removes half or more of the telemetry behind a key metric
templates.subtopic: consent, bias, honest communication with leadership

metric: weekly active devices using a new built-in search feature
a monthly app reliability score reported to the product's leadership
the adoption figure for a productivity feature in the quarterly business review

sections.scenario: Your team owns the data behind {{metric}}. It is computed from optional diagnostic data, which devices send only when their users allow it. A redesigned privacy settings page, shipped by another team, now asks every user to choose again, and the share of devices still sending optional data has fallen from about two thirds to about {{remaining}}. The metric fell sharply the week the change shipped. The product's leaders are asking whether something real changed, and the next review that depends on the metric is in {{weeks}} weeks. One product manager has suggested making the optional-data prompt "less prominent".
sections.problem: How would you handle it? Cover how you establish what actually changed (the product or the measurement), what you tell leadership first and when, how you rebuild a metric that is honest about the smaller and different population, which parts can move to data every device sends and which cannot, how you respond to the suggestion about the prompt, and how you stop the next settings change from surprising you. Then tell me about a real time a change in data collection or definition broke a metric you owned, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: Users' consent choices are not to be worked around, nudged against or inferred. Required diagnostic data, which every device sends, is minimal and may not contain the feature's usage events. You do not own the settings page or the consent design. The privacy team must approve any new use of data.
sections.assumptions: The situation and figures are hypothetical. Nothing here describes any product's actual consent design or data categories.
sections.criteria: Diagnoses measurement versus behaviour with evidence before reporting; communicates early and honestly, with what is known and unknown; rebuilds the metric with explicit uncertainty and bias checks, or redefines it, with a clear break in the series; respects consent absolutely and declines to nudge users, while keeping the relationship with the product manager; works through the privacy team for any new data use; puts in place an early-warning path for consent and settings changes; real example with measurable effect and personal contribution, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Do the devices that still send optional data look like the rest?
clarifications.a: You do not know yet; early signs are that they skew towards managed business devices and enthusiasts.

clarifications.q: Is there any signal from every device?
clarifications.a: Required data includes device counts by build and a few basic health signals; it does not include feature usage.

clarifications.q: Who decides how the metric is reported?
clarifications.a: The product's leadership, on your recommendation.

clarifications.q: Was the settings change announced to your team?
clarifications.a: It was in a release note that nobody on your team read.

hints: Separate the measurement change from any real change: look at metrics that did not depend on optional data, and at the devices whose consent did not change.
A smaller sample is not the problem; a biased one is. Decide what you can estimate, with what uncertainty, and say so.
Treat the discontinuity as a fact to report, not a number to smooth over.
followups: What do you tell the product's leaders in the first 48 hours, and what do you deliberately not claim yet?
How would you estimate the metric for all devices from the {{remaining}} that still report, and how would you check the estimate?
The product manager presses on making the prompt less prominent. What do you say, and to whom?
What would you change so that the next consent or settings change is known to your team before it ships?
In your real example, what did you personally do, and what did the people who used the metric decide differently because of it?

rules.ask: The devices that still report differ from the rest in ways you can only partly observe. How would you know your weighting is wrong?
Making the prompt less prominent would raise the number. Why is that not your call to make, and how do you say no without ending the conversation?
Moving the metric to data every device sends needs the privacy team's approval and may not be appropriate. What would you ask them, and what would you accept as an answer?
A leader screenshots the chart without the footnote and shows the drop to their own leadership. What should have been different?
What did you personally decide or say, and to whom?

templates.title: Integrating an acquired company's data stack without losing its best people
templates.subtopic: migration planning, retention, respecting a different engineering culture

their_stack: self-hosted open-source tools on their own servers
managed services on a different public cloud
one large database and years of hand-written scripts

sections.scenario: Your company has acquired {{acquired}}. Its {{engineers}} data and platform engineers run {{their_stack}}, which works for them and which they are proud of. Leadership wants the acquired product's data on the company's own cloud platform and in the shared reporting within {{months}} months, partly because a hosting contract ends then. You have been asked to lead the data integration. Two of the acquired company's most senior engineers have told a colleague they will leave if they are "told to rewrite everything in someone else's tools".
sections.problem: How would you lead it? Cover how you learn what the acquired stack does and why before proposing anything, what must move by the deadline and what can wait, how you decide what to keep, replace or run side by side, how you involve the acquired engineers in those decisions, how you keep their product reliable for its customers during the move, and how you would know you are losing people before they resign. Then tell me about a real time you led a migration or integration across teams with different ways of working, with its outcome, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: The hosting contract end date is fixed. The acquired product's customers must not see an outage or a data loss. You do not manage the acquired engineers; their own leader does. Security and compliance reviews of the acquired stack must pass before it connects to shared systems.
sections.assumptions: The situation and figures are hypothetical, and no real acquisition is described.
sections.criteria: Learns the existing stack and its reasons before proposing; separates the hard deadline from optional changes; a phased plan with parallel runs, reconciliation and rollback that protects the product's customers; involves the acquired engineers in decisions with real ownership and visible credit; works through their leader rather than around them; treats retention as a leadership responsibility with early signals; handles slippage with explicit trade-offs; real example with measurable outcome and personal contribution, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Has anyone mapped the acquired stack?
clarifications.a: Not formally. Their engineers know it well; the documentation is thin.

clarifications.q: Is a full rewrite expected?
clarifications.a: Leadership expects the data on the company's platform; how is your proposal.

clarifications.q: What does "shared reporting" need?
clarifications.a: A handful of business metrics computed the same way as for the company's other products.

clarifications.q: Do the acquired engineers have a say?
clarifications.a: Formally, only through their leader. In practice, nothing will work without them.

hints: Inventory before opinions: what runs, what it costs, what depends on it, and which parts carry the most risk.
The deadline applies to hosting, not to every tool. Separate what must move from what you would like to change.
Give the acquired engineers ownership of decisions inside clear constraints, and make their expertise visible to the wider organisation.
followups: What do you do in your first two weeks, and whom do you meet first?
Their scheduling tool is better than the company's for their workloads. Do you keep it? On what evidence, and who decides?
Halfway through, the migration is a month behind. What do you cut or change, and how do you tell leadership?
One of the two senior engineers resigns anyway. What do you do that week?
In your real example, what did you get wrong about the other team's way of working, and how did you find out?

rules.ask: Which of those replacements is needed by the deadline, and which is your preference? What would the acquired engineers say about each?
Moving as it is meets the deadline. What risk do you carry afterwards, and when do you pay it down?
What would you see in the first month that tells you someone is about to leave, and what can you actually do about it without managing them?
How long do you run both, how do you decide the new one is correct, and what does running both cost?
Which decision did you personally make, and which did you leave to the acquired engineers?

templates.title: The team's budget is cut by a third — deciding what stops
templates.subtopic: stopping work, stakeholder communication, cost evidence

commitments: usage reports for tenant administrators, an internal metrics platform and a long-running migration
a data export that enterprise customers download, a feature experiment platform and a set of executive dashboards
a nightly data pipeline for a billing system, an anomaly detection service and a self-serve query service

sections.scenario: You lead a data platform team of {{team}} engineers that spends about {{cloud}} a year on cloud compute and storage. It runs {{commitments}}, plus dozens of smaller pipelines, reports and requests built up over years. Next financial year the team's budget, people and cloud spend together, is cut by a third. You are asked to come back in three weeks with what the team will stop doing, what it will do differently, and what the cut will cost the people who depend on you.
sections.problem: How would you decide and carry it out? Cover what evidence you gather (usage, cost, who depends on what, what is required by contract or law), how you decide what stops, what is reduced and what is protected, how you find savings that do not stop anything, how you involve your team and how you tell the people who lose something, how you shut things down safely, and how you look after the team through it. Then tell me about a real time you had to stop work that someone valued, with its outcome, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: Some outputs are promised to customers in their contracts. People decisions follow the company's own process, which you do not control. The cut is decided; your job is how it lands. Nothing is switched off without notice to its users.
sections.assumptions: The situation and figures are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Evidence first (inventory with cost, users, dependencies and contractual or legal obligations); efficiency savings separated from stopping work and estimated honestly; explicit criteria for stopping, reducing and protecting; safe shutdowns with notice, alternatives, scream tests where appropriate and a way back; honest communication with stakeholders and escalation of real trade-offs; care for the team within the company's process; real example with measurable outcome and personal contribution, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Do you know who uses each report and pipeline?
clarifications.a: Partly. Query logs and access logs exist; nobody has joined them to the list of outputs.

clarifications.q: Can the cut come only from cloud spend?
clarifications.a: Partly; how much is up to your evidence. The cut covers both.

clarifications.q: Will stakeholders accept less?
clarifications.a: Some will; several will escalate.

clarifications.q: Is the team aware?
clarifications.a: There are rumours; nothing has been said officially.

hints: Build one list of everything the team runs, with cost, users, last use and what breaks if it stops.
Look for waste before value: unused outputs, over-provisioned compute, data kept far longer than any use requires.
Stopping something well is work: notice, an alternative or an export, a date, and a way back if you were wrong.
followups: Walk me through how you would rank the team's outputs. What does each one's score depend on?
A senior leader's favourite dashboard costs more than it is worth by your measure. What do you do?
How much of the cut can come from efficiency (compute, storage, retention) before anything stops, and how do you check the estimate?
After you switch off a pipeline, a team you did not know about says their monthly report is broken. What happens next?
In your real example, what did you stop, who objected, and what did stopping it actually save or cost?

rules.ask: A report is opened once a quarter, by the finance team, for a filing. Does low usage mean low value?
What does an equal cut to every service do to the ones that cannot run at two thirds?
Which efficiency saving is realistic within the year, and what does it cost the team to deliver it while also absorbing the cut?
What notice do the users get, what do they move to, and how do you find the users you do not know about?
What do you tell the team before the decisions are final, and what do you keep to yourself?

templates.title: Leading a cross-organisation working group with no authority over its members
templates.subtopic: shared standards across product groups, decision-making

goal: one definition of an active user that every product group reports the same way
a shared schema for usage events that product groups send to a common store
a common retention standard for diagnostic and usage data across product groups

sections.scenario: Leadership has asked for {{goal}}, and has asked you to lead a working group of engineers and analysts from {{groups}} product groups (chat and meetings, mail and calendar, documents, the operating system and others) to deliver it in {{months}} months. None of the members report to you; each has their own manager, roadmap and reasons why their product is different. Two earlier attempts at the same thing ended with a document nobody followed.
sections.problem: How would you lead it? Cover how you find out why the earlier attempts failed, how you set up the group (who, how often, how decisions are made and recorded), how you get from {{groups}} different practices to one standard, how you handle a product group that disagrees or does not show up, how you get the standard adopted and not just agreed, and how you will know it worked. Then tell me about a real time you led a group of peers who did not report to you to a decision, with its outcome, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: You have no authority over the members or their roadmaps. Leadership will back a decision but will not make it for you. Each product group's existing reports must keep working while it moves to the standard.
sections.assumptions: The situation and figures are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Learns from the failed attempts before starting; makes the problem concrete with evidence; sets up the group with the right representatives, a clear decision process and a written record; reaches a decision that allows justified differences while keeping numbers comparable; handles disengaged groups through their managers and leadership sponsorship without coercion; drives adoption with tooling, pilots, migration plans and an owner for the standard; measures success by adoption and agreement of numbers; real example with outcome and personal contribution, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Why did the earlier attempts fail?
clarifications.a: People give different reasons; that is for you to find out.

clarifications.q: Does each product group have someone empowered to agree?
clarifications.a: Some sent senior engineers who can commit; others sent whoever was free.

clarifications.q: Can the standard allow product-specific differences?
clarifications.a: Leadership wants comparable numbers; you decide how much variation is acceptable.

clarifications.q: Who maintains the standard afterwards?
clarifications.a: Undecided.

hints: Make the cost of the current situation concrete with data: where numbers disagree today and what that has led to.
Agree how decisions are made before arguing about the decisions themselves.
Adoption needs a cheap path: tooling, a reference implementation, a migration plan per group, and a named owner afterwards.
followups: What do you do in the first two weeks, before the first meeting of the full group?
Two product groups have incompatible definitions and both are right for their products. How do you get to a decision?
One group's representative stops attending and their manager says the work is not a priority this half. What do you do?
The standard is agreed. Three months later, only two groups have adopted it. What went wrong, and what do you change?
In your real example, what decision did the group make that you would not have made alone?

rules.ask: With {{groups}} groups, what happens when one never agrees? How is the decision made then?
What exactly do you ask leadership for, and what do you lose with the group if you go to them?
The last two attempts produced a document too. What makes yours different on the day after it is agreed?
Which product group goes first, why them, and what do they get out of it?
What did you personally propose, and how did it change in the group?

templates.title: Project deep dive, re-examined for enterprise customers inside compliance boundaries
templates.subtopic: design decisions, failures, enterprise compliance requirements

angle: the data model and why it held up
the hardest correctness problem you solved
the most important reliability decision you made
requirement: each customer's data stored and processed only inside one chosen geography
encryption with keys the customer holds and can revoke at any time
legal holds that stop deletion of a customer's data until the hold is lifted
a complete audit log of every access to customer data that customers can export

sections.scenario: In this part of the loop you describe a data system you designed or substantially changed, one that other teams or customers depended on. The interviewer will go deep on {{angle}}, then ask how the system would have to change to serve {{tenants}} enterprise customer organisations, each of which can require {{requirement}}. The requirement is this exercise's; treat it as a product commitment, and do not reason about what any law demands.
sections.problem: Give a five-minute overview: the problem, the users, the scale in numbers, the architecture and your role. Then go deep on {{angle}}. Then reason through what changes when each of {{tenants}} customer organisations can require {{requirement}}: where data lives and moves, which components are affected (storage, caches, logs, backups, analytics copies, support access), and how you would prove to a customer that the commitment holds. If you have never owned such a system, say so, pick the closest thing you have worked on, and be clear about which parts you are reasoning through rather than recalling.
sections.constraints: Your own project only. Describe it without revealing anything a previous employer would not want shared; round numbers are fine if you say so.
sections.assumptions: The enterprise setting and its requirements are hypothetical and are not legal advice.
sections.criteria: Clear problem framing with real numbers; depth on the chosen angle down to keys, schemas and failure modes; decisions explained with alternatives and evidence; an honest account of what broke and what changed; a complete inventory of where customer data lives, including logs, caches, backups and derived copies; a credible, per-tenant design for the requirement with its cost and failure modes; continuous evidence that the commitment holds; own contribution clearly separated from the team's, or an honest statement of reasoning rather than recall.

clarifications.q: Does it have to be a data system?
clarifications.a: It should move, store or compute data that others depend on; a service with a significant data model counts.

clarifications.q: Can it be a team project?
clarifications.a: Yes, but separate what you did from what the team did.

clarifications.q: How deep should I go?
clarifications.a: Down to keys, schemas, failure modes and numbers.

clarifications.q: Did my system ever serve enterprise customers?
clarifications.a: It does not need to have; the second half is reasoning, and you should say which parts are.

hints: Lead with the problem and the numbers before the architecture.
Have one decision you would defend again and one you would change.
For the enterprise question, list every copy of a customer's data your system makes (including logs, caches, backups and derived tables) before deciding what has to change.
followups: What was the main alternative to your key design decision, and what evidence chose between them?
What broke in production, how did you find out, and what did you change?
Which copies of a customer's data in your system would the requirement affect, and which would you have forgotten at first?
How would you prove to a customer's auditor that the requirement holds, continuously rather than once?
What would you build differently today, and why?

rules.ask: Which parts did you personally design or write?
Why that over the obvious alternative, and what did it cost you?
Is that per day or in total, and what was the peak relative to the average?
A customer revokes access or a hold changes what may be deleted. What happens to the copies in your backups?
Your logs and traces contain identifiers and sometimes payloads. Where do they go, and does the requirement cover them?
